Module 5 · Week 1 — VR: Begin Your Gas Behavior & Energy Lab

This is the first build of the four-week Gas Behavior & Energy Lab, so students should leave with a placed, locked gas-law apparatus, three labeled gauges, a P–V pair note, and a saved snapshot. Common sticking points: students sometimes label the gauges but never use the plunger to show the trade-off — the Boyle demonstration (push in → pressure up) is the heart of the activity, not just the static build. Make sure the labeled P–V pair is internally consistent with the inverse relationship (volume to one-quarter → pressure times four). The activity now runs on the investigation arc (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend): the load-bearing habits are the committed prediction written before the plunger moves and the CER reflection at submission — watch for students who investigate first and back-fill a “prediction” afterward. Grading stays completion-based (they predicted, investigated, and defended a claim with evidence); you are not scoring the claim's polish. Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week 2 measured-amounts/partial-pressure station, the Week 3 KMT particle annotations, and the Week 4 calorimetry setup, all in the same persistent Session. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 5 · Week 1 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Build the Gas-Law Apparatus — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The conceptual heart is the Boyle “before / after”: make sure the smaller volume is paired with the higher pressure, and that the labeled P–V pair is internally consistent with the inverse trade-off (volume to one-quarter → pressure times four). This pathway follows the same objectives and the same completion-based rubric as the OptimaXR version and runs on the same investigation arc (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend): the load-bearing habits are the committed prediction written before the “after” panel and the CER reflection at submission — watch for students who solve first and back-fill a “prediction” afterward. Encourage them to keep the file tidy and leave room; they'll extend it across Weeks 2–4 toward the recorded walkthrough.

Module 5 · Week 2 — VR: Gas-Stoichiometry & Partial-Pressure Station

This is Build 2 of 4 of the cumulative Gas Behavior & Energy Lab, structured as an inquiry arc (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend) that ends in a written CER reflection. Students should leave with a gas-stoichiometry station and a partial-pressure jar added beside last week's gas-law apparatus, all locked, plus a signed prediction note, a signed reasoning note, a saved Gas_Wk2_YourName snapshot, and a Claim–Evidence–Reasoning comment. It stays completion-based — the arc deepens the thinking, it does not add grading. Common sticking points: skipping the Predict step and building straight to the answer (nudge them to commit a prediction first); making the volume blocks the wrong relative sizes (the H2 and H2O stacks must be twice the O2 stack to show 2:1:2); and treating partial pressures as something to average rather than add — the Analyze-step sum is where that gets nailed down. Remind students to leave room to the right for the Week-3 KMT-particle build. The same Location/Session (“Gas & Energy Lab”) must persist across all four weeks. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 5 · Week 2 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Gas-Stoichiometry & Partial-Pressure Station Diagram — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate follows the same inquiry arc as the VR version (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend) and ends in the same written CER reflection, at equal rigor; it stays completion-based. It produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” Watch for three things: skipping the Predict step and drawing straight to the answer (nudge them to commit a prediction first); drawing the volume blocks in the right relative sizes (the H2 and H2O blocks must be twice the O2 block to show 2:1:2); and treating partial pressures as something to average rather than add — the Analyze-step sum is where that gets pinned down. Encourage students to keep extending one cumulative file across the module rather than starting fresh each week.

Module 5 · Week 3 — VR: See the Particles Move

This is Build 3 of 4 of the cumulative Gas & Energy Lab; students should leave with a particle swarm inside the existing cylinder, two KMT sticky notes (one signed), a light-vs-heavy diffusion/effusion observation, and a saved Gas_Wk3_YourName snapshot. Common sticking points: students sometimes pack the particles tightly — remind them a gas is mostly empty space, so the particles should be far apart and small; and some conflate kinetic energy (equal for all gases at one temperature) with speed (greater for the lighter gas) — the two sticky notes are meant to hold both ideas side by side. Make sure the cumulative scene uses the same Location/Session as Weeks 1, 2, and 4 so the build persists, and that students leave open floor space for the Week-4 calorimetry setup and final recording. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 5 · Week 3 — VR Non-VR Alternate: See the Particles Move — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” Watch for two things: students sometimes pack the particles tightly — remind them a gas is mostly empty space, so the dots should be small and far apart; and some conflate kinetic energy (equal for all gases at one temperature) with speed (greater for the lighter gas) — the two labels are meant to hold both ideas side by side. Encourage students to keep the project file tidy; they'll add the calorimetry setup and the recording in Week 4.

Module 5 · Week 4 — VR: Build 4 of 4 — Gas & Energy Lab

This is the final build of the four-week Gas & Energy Lab and the bridge into the graded module VR project (the recorded video). Students should leave with a complete, locked four-station exhibit and a saved Gas_Final_YourName snapshot. Common sticking points: drawing the heat arrow the wrong way (heat flows from the hot metal into the cooler water, never the reverse), and confusing temperature change with total heat (the water and metal reach the same final temperature, but their q values are equal and opposite, not their ΔT values). Remind students that this weekly piece is completion-only; the accuracy and depth of their spoken explanation is assessed in the separate module VR project. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 5 · Week 4 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Calorimetry Station & Record Prep — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions and serves as the storyboard for the student's recorded module project. Watch for the same two sticking points as the VR build: drawing the heat arrow the wrong way (heat flows from the hot metal into the cooler water), and confusing temperature change with total heat (water and metal reach the same final temperature, but it's their q values that are equal and opposite, not their ΔT values). This weekly piece is completion-only; the depth of the spoken explanation is assessed in the separate module VR project alternate.

Module 5 — Writing Assignment: Calorimetry: A Lab Report

This lab report is one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 5. For reference, the data set resolves cleanly: qwater = (100.0)(4.184)(23.5 − 20.0) = (100.0)(4.184)(3.5) = 1464 J gained, so qmetal = −1464 J. With ΔTmetal = 23.5 − 100.0 = −76.5 °C, cmetal = 1464 ÷ (50.0 × 76.5) = 1464 ÷ 3825 = 0.383 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹, which matches copper (table value 0.385). The most common errors: using the water's specific heat for the metal, using the wrong ΔT (metal's vs water's), losing track of signs, and forgetting that |qmetal| = qwater. Reward complete, unit-carried, sign-correct work and an honest error discussion (real-world losses to the cup and air make the measured c slightly off) over a lucky final number. Watch for AI-generated reports that state a specific heat with no shown q = mcΔT work — ask for the student's own calculation. Grade from the rubric; keep written comments brief and aimed at the reasoning.

Module 5 — VR Project: Gas Behavior & Energy Lab: Recorded Walkthrough

This is the capstone of the four-week build and one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 5. The assessed work is the narrated explanation, so coach students to reason aloud — especially the through-line that measurement plus conservation is the discipline of the quantitative, the distinction between a measured gas law and the KMT theory that explains it, and the conservation-of-energy logic at the calorimeter (qmetal = −qwater). Common sticking points: forgetting that gas-law temperatures must be in kelvin, confusing total pressure with a single partial pressure, claiming the heavier gas effuses faster, and starting the OptimaXR video recording (demonstrate the menu/tablet capture). Offer the screen-recording fallback for audio. Finished submissions can be gathered into a teacher-assembled gallery Location for a class walk. Grade from the rubric above; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Module 5 — VR Project Non-VR Alternate: Gas Behavior & Energy Lab — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)

This alternate produces a narrated video that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The assessed work is the reasoning, not the production quality — coach students to explain why (P and V are inversely related at constant T; total pressure is the sum of partials; lighter molecules effuse faster; qmetal = −qwater because energy is conserved) rather than just naming parts. Option B's hot-water-and-thermometer demonstration is a genuine calorimetry observation and should be encouraged. Grade from the same rubric as the VR pathway; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Module 6 · Week 1 — VR: Begin Your Intermolecular Forces & States Model

This is the first build of the three-week Intermolecular Forces & States Model, so students should leave with three placed, locked and labeled force models, a signed summary note, and a saved snapshot. Common sticking points: students sometimes draw a “hydrogen bond” on a molecule that can't form one — make sure the hydrogen bond is between two water molecules (H on O), and that HCl is correctly labeled dipole-dipole, not hydrogen bonding (its H is on chlorine). The conceptual heart is the strength order tied to boiling point, not just three pretty models. The activity now runs on the investigation arc (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend): the load-bearing habits are the committed ranking written before the models go up and the CER reflection at submission — watch for students who build first and back-fill a “prediction” afterward. Grading stays completion-based (they predicted, built, and defended a claim with evidence); you are not scoring the claim's polish. Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week 2 crystal lattice / dissolution station and the Week 3 property-explanation annotations, all in the same persistent Session. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 6 · Week 1 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Model the Three Forces — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The conceptual heart is the strength order tied to boiling point, not just three diagrams. The activity runs on the investigation arc (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend): the load-bearing habits are the committed ranking written before the diagrams and the CER reflection at submission — watch for students who draw first and back-fill a “prediction” afterward. Grading stays completion-based (they predicted, drew, and defended a claim with evidence); you are not scoring the claim's polish. Watch for the common error of labeling HCl as “hydrogen bonding” — its H is on chlorine, so it is dipole-dipole; hydrogen bonding belongs only to the two-water diagram (H on O). Encourage them to keep the file tidy and leave room; they'll extend it across Weeks 2–3 toward the recorded walkthrough.

Module 6 · Week 2 — VR: Crystal Lattice & Dissolution Station

This is the second build of the three-week Intermolecular Forces & States Model, added to the same persistent States & Solutions Lab Session as Week 1, so students should leave with their Week-1 IMF models still in place plus a placed, locked crystal lattice and dissolution station, labels, and a saved IMF_Wk2_YourName snapshot. The activity now runs on the investigation arc (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend): the load-bearing habits are the committed prediction written before the water reaches the lattice and the CER reflection at submission — watch for students who build the dissolution first and back-fill a “prediction” afterward. Common sticking points: students sometimes build a pretty lattice but never show the water actually pulling ions off — the hydration moment (water's charged ends orienting toward the ions, ions drifting free) is the heart of the activity, not just a static grid. Check that the water dipoles are oriented correctly (negative oxygen toward the positive ion, positive hydrogens toward the negative ion) and that the strong-electrolyte vs nonelectrolyte contrast is clearly labeled. Grading stays completion-based (they predicted, investigated, and defended a claim with evidence); you are not scoring the claim's polish. Remind students to leave room for the Week 3 property-explanation annotations before the recorded walkthrough. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 6 · Week 2 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Build a Crystal Lattice & Dissolution Station — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” This pathway now runs on the same investigation arc as the VR version (Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend): the load-bearing habits are the committed prediction written before the dissolution is drawn and the CER reflection at submission — watch for students who draw first and back-fill a “prediction” afterward, and keep grading completion-based (not scoring the claim's polish). The conceptual heart is the dissolution diagram: make sure the water dipoles are oriented correctly (negative oxygen toward the positive ion, positive hydrogens toward the negative ion) and that the strong-electrolyte vs nonelectrolyte contrast is clearly labeled — a static lattice alone isn't enough; the water must be shown pulling ions off. Encourage them to keep the file tidy and add to the same document each week toward the recorded walkthrough.

Module 6 · Week 3 — VR: Finish Your IMF & States Model

This is the third and final build of the three-week IMF & States Model, so students should leave with a complete model: Week-1 IMF models, Week-2 lattice + dissolution station, and now Week-3 property-explanation annotations, with an IMF_Final_YourName snapshot ready for the recorded walkthrough (the module project). The heart of this build is the cause → effect reasoning — tying micro structure to macro property — not adding more objects. Common sticking points: students sometimes write the property (e.g. “ice floats”) without naming the cause (the open hydrogen-bonded lattice), or get the colligative arithmetic wrong — check that 1.00 m NaCl gives ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C (FP −3.72 °C), i.e. i = 2, not 1. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity in the persistent States & Solutions Lab Session.

Module 6 · Week 3 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Add Property-Explanation Annotations — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a completed file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions and narrated for the module project, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The conceptual heart is the cause → effect reasoning — tying micro structure to a macro property — not adding more art. Watch for two things: students naming a property without its cause (e.g. “ice floats” with no mention of the open hydrogen-bonded lattice), and colligative-math slips — confirm 1.00 m NaCl gives ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C (i = 2, FP −3.72 °C).

Module 6 — Writing Assignment: Why Matter Behaves: A Scientific Argument

This argument is one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 6. Prompt A reference: all three molecules have London dispersion; ethane (C2H6, nonpolar) has only dispersion (boils lowest, −89 °C); formaldehyde (CH2O, polar C=O) adds dipole-dipole (−19 °C); ethanol (C2H5OH) has an –OH and so hydrogen-bonds (highest, +78 °C) — the order tracks IMF strength. Prompt B reference: 1.00 m NaCl, i = 2 → ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C, freezing at −3.72 °C; 1.00 m CaCl2, i = 3 → ΔTf = 3 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 5.58 °C, freezing at −5.58 °C — more particles, more depression, which is why CaCl2 works on colder nights. The most common errors: forgetting London dispersion is present in every molecule, calling a single –OH a “dipole” without naming hydrogen bonding, and dropping the van’t Hoff factor i. Reward arguments built from the molecular level with shown math — and a counter-case answered with evidence (mass vs IMF type in A; particle count vs mere dissolving in B) — over a correct answer asserted without evidence. Watch for AI-generated arguments that name forces a structure doesn't support — ask for the student's own structural reasoning. Grade from the rubric; keep written comments brief and aimed at the reasoning.

Module 6 — VR Project: Intermolecular Forces & States Model: Recorded Walkthrough

This is the capstone of the three-week build and one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 6. The assessed work is the narrated explanation, so coach students to reason aloud — especially the through-line that the properties we measure are written into the forces between molecules, the strength order of the three IMFs, and the model→property links (open hydrogen-bonded lattice → ice floats; dissolved particles → freezing-point depression, ΔTf = i·Kf·m), and one honest limit (“like dissolves like” and colligative ideality are models that break down for real solutions). The top rubric criterion is evidence-based scientific reasoning, so weight the grade toward explanations tied to the evidence over parts merely named. Common sticking points: drawing a “hydrogen bond” as a covalent bond inside one molecule rather than an attraction between molecules; claiming London dispersion only exists in nonpolar substances (it's in all of them); confusing a strong electrolyte (free ions) with a nonelectrolyte (whole molecules); and starting the OptimaXR video recording (demonstrate the menu/tablet capture). Offer the screen-recording fallback for audio. Finished submissions can be gathered into a teacher-assembled gallery Location for a class walk. Grade from the rubric above; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Module 6 — VR Project Non-VR Alternate: Intermolecular Forces & States Model — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)

This alternate produces a narrated video that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The assessed work is the reasoning, not the production quality — coach students to explain why (stronger IMFs raise the boiling point; an ionic lattice is brittle and conducts only when free to move; salt water conducts because it has free ions; dissolved particles lower the freezing point) rather than just naming parts, and to name one honest limit (“like dissolves like” and colligative ideality are models that break down for real solutions). The top rubric criterion is evidence-based scientific reasoning, so weight the grade toward explanations tied to the evidence. Option B's salt-water-vs-sugar-water and floating-ice demonstrations are genuine observations and should be encouraged. Grade from the same rubric as the VR pathway; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Module 7 · Week 1 — VR: Entropy & Spontaneity Sort

This build follows an investigation arc — Observe, Question, Predict, Investigate, Analyze, Defend, Extend — and ends with a short CER reflection. The committed prediction before building is the point: students should post it and leave it unchanged so the Analyze step has something to test against. Students should leave with a committed Prediction note, two correctly sorted sets of bins (entropy and spontaneity) with reason notes, a signed anchor note, a saved snapshot, and a three-sentence CER. Common sticking points: students sometimes conflate entropy direction with spontaneity — remind them these are sorted separately (a process can lower the system's entropy and still be spontaneous, like water freezing), and that spontaneity is about direction, not speed. The conceptual heart is reasoning why from the ΔS sign rules and the ΔSuniv > 0 anchor, not just dropping cards in bins. Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week 2–5 builds, all in the same persistent Equilibrium & Acids Lab Session. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 7 · Week 1 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Entropy & Spontaneity Sort — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate follows the same investigation arc as the VR version — Observe, Question, Predict, Investigate, Analyze, Defend, Extend — and ends with a short CER reflection, so it meets the same objectives at equal rigor. The committed prediction before building is the point: students should write it and leave it unchanged so the Analyze step has something to test against. It produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The conceptual heart is reasoning why from the ΔS sign rules and the ΔSuniv > 0 anchor, not just placing words in boxes. Watch for the common error of conflating entropy direction with spontaneity — they are sorted separately, and a process can lower the system's entropy yet still be spontaneous (water freezing). Encourage them to keep the file tidy and leave room; they'll extend it across Weeks 2–5 toward the recorded walkthrough.

Module 7 · Week 2 — VR: Reversible-Reaction Equilibrium Demo

This is Build 2 of 5 of the cumulative Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station, built in the same persistent Session (Equilibrium & Acids Lab) so the project accumulates week to week. Students should leave with last week's sort still present plus a new, locked equilibrium demo, a signed summary note, and the EqAcid_Wk2_YourName snapshot. The most common misconception to catch: students saying equilibrium means the reaction “stopped” or that reactant and product amounts are “equal” — the correct idea is equal rates and constant (not necessarily equal) concentrations, in a closed system. Make sure the two rate arrows are drawn the same length. Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week 3 Le Châtelier panel, the Week 4 pH scale, and the Week 5 titration station. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 7 · Week 2 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Reversible-Reaction Equilibrium Demo — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” It is Build 2 of 5 of the same growing project — students should be extending last week's file, not starting over. The most common misconception to catch: equating equilibrium with the reaction “stopping,” or thinking reactant and product amounts must be equal — the correct idea is equal rates and constant (not necessarily equal) concentrations in a closed system. Make sure the two rate arrows are drawn the same length. Encourage them to keep the file tidy and leave room for the Weeks 3–5 exhibits leading to the recorded walkthrough.

Module 7 · Week 3 — VR: Le Châtelier Shift Narration

This is the third build of the five-week Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station, layered onto the same persistent Session so the station accumulates. The activity runs on a scientist's arc — observe, question, commit a prediction before investigating, then analyze and defend with a CER card. Insist on the committed prediction in Step 2 before any building; the value is in students being surprised and then correcting themselves. Students should leave with a stress panel showing three correctly-directed shifts, a signed catalyst note, a CER card, and a saved EqAcid_Wk3_YourName snapshot. Common sticking points: the temperature shift trips students up — make sure they first commit to whether the demo is exothermic or endothermic, then place heat on the correct side before predicting the shift; and the catalyst note must say “no shift,” not “shifts right.” The conceptual heart is “the system partially counteracts each stress,” not just three pretty arrows. Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week-4 pH & indicator station and the Week-5 titration setup, all in the same Location. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 7 · Week 3 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Le Châtelier Shift Narration — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen,” and it carries equal rigor: the same scientist's arc — observe, question, commit a prediction before investigating, analyze, and defend with a CER. Insist on the committed prediction in Step 2 before any diagramming; the value is in students being surprised and then correcting themselves. The conceptual heart is “the system partially counteracts each stress,” not just three arrows. Watch for two common errors: students often get the temperature shift backwards — have them commit to exo/endo and place heat on the correct side first; and the catalyst note must say “no shift.” Encourage them to keep the file tidy and leave room; they'll extend it across Weeks 4–5 toward the recorded walkthrough.

Module 7 · Week 4 — VR: pH & Indicator Station

This is Build 4 of 5 of the cumulative Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station, all in the same persistent Session so the project accumulates toward the Week-5 recorded walkthrough. Students should leave with a labeled pH scale, at least one strong acid / weak acid / strong base correctly placed and annotated, indicator swatches, a signed relationships panel, and a saved EqAcid_Wk4_YourName snapshot. Common sticking points: students sometimes conflate “strong” with “concentrated” — make sure their labels describe how completely the acid/base ionizes, not how much is present; and watch for a weak acid placed too low on the scale. Remind them to leave space at the far end of the rail for the Week-5 titration setup. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 7 · Week 4 — VR Non-VR Alternate: pH & Indicator Station — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The conceptual heart is the pH scale's structure (neutral 7, lower pH = more acidic) and the strong-vs-weak distinction tied to placement on the scale. Watch for the common error of conflating “strong” with “concentrated” — labels should describe how completely the acid/base ionizes. Encourage them to keep the project file tidy and extend it next week toward the recorded walkthrough (Build 5 of 5).

Module 7 · Week 5 — VR: Titration Station (Build 5 of 5) + record

This is the final build of the five-week Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station and the week students record the project walkthrough. Students should leave with a locked, labeled titration station, a saved EqAcid_Final_YourName snapshot, a completion screenshot + caption here, and a recorded video submitted to the separate graded Module VR Project. Common sticking points: students sometimes call the indicator color change the “cause” of the equivalence point — clarify it only signals it; and some forget MaVa = MbVb assumes a 1:1 reaction. Encourage clear narration over a polished model: the assessed work in the project is the spoken explanation. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 7 · Week 5 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Titration Station — No-Headset Pathway (+ narrated recording)

This alternate produces a file and a narrated recording that mirror the VR project exactly, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The assessed work in the project is the spoken explanation, so encourage clear narration over a polished diagram. Watch for two common errors: treating the indicator color change as the cause (rather than the signal) of the equivalence point, and forgetting that MaVa = MbVb assumes a 1:1 reaction. The recorded walkthrough goes to the separate graded Module VR Project; this weekly assignment just collects the finished file + caption.

Module 7 — Writing Assignment: Equilibrium Under Pressure: A Le Chatelier CER

This CER is one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 7. Prompt A reference: adding CO2 (a reactant) shifts CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− to the right, raising [H+], which lowers pH (the ocean becomes more acidic); the added H+ also shifts the bicarbonate/carbonate equilibrium so less CO32− is available, starving corals, oysters, and plankton of the carbonate they need for CaCO3 shells. Prompt B reference: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 goes 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas, so high pressure favors NH3; ΔH = −92 kJ/mol is exothermic, so low temperature favors NH3 — but low temperature makes the rate impractically slow, so industry compromises (~400–450 °C, ~150–300 atm, iron catalyst); cheap ammonia for fertilizer underwrites the food supply of billions (Haber, 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Bosch scaled it up). The most common errors: predicting a shift toward more gas moles under pressure, flipping the temperature rule for an exothermic reaction, and claiming more H+ raises pH. Reward arguments built from the balanced equilibrium with each shift justified by a named rule over a correct guess with no chemistry. Watch for AI-generated CERs that reverse a shift — ask the student to re-derive it from Le Châtelier's principle. Grade from the rubric; keep written comments brief and aimed at the reasoning.

Module 7 — VR Project: Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station: Recorded Walkthrough

This is the capstone of the five-week build and one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 7. The assessed work is the narrated explanation, so coach students to reason aloud — especially the through-line from spontaneity & entropy (ΔSuniv > 0; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS) through dynamic equilibrium & K, the Le Châtelier shifts (Haber: high P and low T favor NH3), the pH scale and strong-vs-weak distinction, and the titration to equivalence (MaVa = MbVb, worked 0.120 M HCl). Common sticking points: saying equilibrium means the reaction has “stopped” (it hasn't — the rates are equal); predicting a pressure shift toward more gas moles; flipping the temperature rule for an exothermic reaction; confusing acid strength (degree of ionization) with concentration; and confusing the equivalence point with a pH of 7 for a weak-acid titration (it's > 7 there). Demonstrate the OptimaXR video-recording menu/tablet capture, and offer the screen-recording fallback for audio. Finished submissions can be gathered into a teacher-assembled gallery Location for a class walk. Grade from the rubric above; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Module 7 — VR Project Non-VR Alternate: Equilibrium & Acid-Base Station — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)

This alternate produces a narrated video that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The assessed work is the reasoning, not the production quality — coach students to explain why (ΔSuniv > 0 and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decide spontaneity; equilibrium means equal rates, not a stopped reaction; add a reactant shifts right; high pressure favors fewer gas moles; for the exothermic Haber reaction low T favors NH3; a strong acid is fully ionized while a weak acid is only partly ionized; the equivalence point is where moles of base equal moles of acid) rather than just naming parts. Option B's real titration and red-cabbage pH strip are genuine observations and should be encouraged. Common errors: confusing acid strength with concentration, and claiming equilibrium means the reaction stopped. Grade from the same rubric as the VR pathway; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Teacher notes for the Module 8 assignments. Not for students.

Module 8 · Week 1 — VR: Galvanic Cell Foundation

This is the first build of the four-week Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build, so students should leave with a complete galvanic cell — two half-cells, a salt bridge, an external wire, correctly labeled anode/cathode with signs, an electron-flow arrow, and a signed anchor note — plus a saved snapshot. Common sticking points: students often reverse the electron-flow direction (electrons go anode → cathode) or mix up which electrode is which (“An Ox, Red Cat”); a few forget the salt bridge entirely and think the wire alone is enough. The conceptual heart is that a galvanic cell separates a spontaneous redox reaction so its electrons are forced through the wire — not just assembling parts. Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week 2–4 builds, all in the same persistent Electrochem & Rates Lab Session. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 8 · Week 1 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Galvanic Cell Foundation — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The conceptual heart is that a galvanic cell separates a spontaneous redox reaction so its electrons are forced through the wire — not just drawing labeled parts. Watch for two common errors: reversing the electron-flow direction (electrons travel anode → cathode) and mixing up the electrodes (“An Ox, Red Cat”). Encourage students to keep the file tidy and leave room; they'll extend it across Weeks 2–4 toward the recorded walkthrough.

Module 8 · Week 2 — VR: Cell Potential Panel

This is Build 2 of 4 of the cumulative Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build, built in the same persistent Session (Electrochem & Rates Lab, spawn Lab Bench A) so the project accumulates week to week. Students should leave with last week's galvanic cell still present plus a new, locked Cell Potential Panel, a signed through-line note, and the ElectroRate_Wk2_YourName snapshot. The most common misconceptions to catch: ranking the strip upside-down (most-negative on top), and the double-negative slip when reasoning that E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = +1.10 V (not −0.42 V). Confirm the strongest oxidizer (Ag+, +0.80) sits at the top. The build now runs on an Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend arc — the load-bearing move is the committed prediction in Step 3, made before the voltmeter is spawned, and the closing CER reflection; nudge students who skip straight to placing the meter. Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week 3 real-cells & electrolysis build and the Week 4 rate & catalysis demo. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 8 · Week 2 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Cell Potential Panel — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” It is Build 2 of 4 of the same growing project — students should be extending last week's file, not starting over. The most common misconceptions to catch: ranking the strip upside-down (most-negative on top), and the double-negative slip in E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = +1.10 V (not −0.42 V). Confirm the strongest oxidizer (Ag+, +0.80) sits at the top and that the higher-E° half-reaction is named the cathode. This alternate now runs on the same Observe → Question → Predict → Investigate → Analyze → Defend → Extend arc as the VR version — the load-bearing move is the committed prediction in Step 3, made before the +1.10 V reading is drawn, and the closing CER reflection; nudge students who skip straight to writing the answer. Encourage them to keep the file tidy and leave room for the Weeks 3–4 exhibits leading to the recorded walkthrough.

Module 8 · Week 3 — VR: Real Cells & Electrolysis Panel

This is the third build of the four-week Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build, layered onto the same persistent Session so the station accumulates. Students should leave with a real-cells panel (battery primary/secondary, fuel cell, corrosion / sacrificial anode, electrolytic cell), a signed galvanic-vs-electrolytic note, and a saved ElectroRate_Wk3_YourName snapshot. Common sticking points: students often flip the electrolytic-cell signs incorrectly — remind them that oxidation is always at the anode in both cell types, and only the +/− labels flip; and the corrosion note should say the sacrificial metal is oxidized instead of the iron (it doesn't “protect” by magic). The conceptual heart is the contrast “galvanic makes electricity, electrolytic uses it.” Remind students to leave bench room to the right for the Week-4 rate & catalysis demo and the final recording, all in the same Location. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 8 · Week 3 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Real Cells & Electrolysis Panel — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The conceptual heart is the contrast “galvanic makes electricity, electrolytic uses it,” with the four real cells as concrete examples. Watch for two common errors: students often flip the electrolytic-cell signs wrong — remind them oxidation is always at the anode in both cell types and only the +/− labels flip; and the corrosion note should say the sacrificial metal is oxidized instead of the iron. Encourage them to keep the file tidy and leave room; they'll extend it in Week 4 toward the recorded walkthrough.

Module 8 · Week 4 — VR: Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo (Build 4 of 4) + record

This is the final build of the four-week Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build and the week students record the project walkthrough. Students should leave with a locked, labeled rate/catalysis demo, a saved ElectroRate_Final_YourName snapshot, a completion screenshot + caption here, and a recorded video submitted to the separate graded Module VR Project. Common sticking points: students sometimes say a catalyst “makes the reaction release more energy” or “shifts the equilibrium” — clarify it lowers Ea and changes only the rate, not ΔG, the equilibrium, or the products; and some conflate spontaneity with speed — reinforce “thermodynamics gives direction, kinetics gives speed.” Encourage clear narration over a polished model: the assessed work in the project is the spoken explanation. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 8 · Week 4 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Reaction-Rate & Catalysis Demo — No-Headset Pathway (+ narrated recording)

This alternate produces a file and a narrated recording that mirror the VR project exactly, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The assessed work in the project is the spoken explanation, so encourage clear narration over a polished diagram. Watch for two common errors: claiming a catalyst “makes the reaction release more energy” or “shifts the equilibrium” (it lowers Ea and changes only the rate), and conflating spontaneity with speed (thermodynamics gives direction, kinetics gives speed). The recorded walkthrough goes to the separate graded Module VR Project; this weekly assignment just collects the finished file + caption.

Module 8 — Writing Assignment: Powering the Future: A Battery Argument

This argument is one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 8. There is no single “right” chemistry — reward the quality of the electrochemical reasoning and the honesty of the trade-off analysis, not the choice itself. Reference fits: for the EV (A), lithium-ion is the natural pick (high energy density, rechargeable, many cycles), with the honest cost being lithium/cobalt sourcing and recycling; for grid storage (B), lead-acid (cheap, reliable, weight irrelevant) or lithium-ion both defend well; for the disposable device (C), an alkaline primary cell (~1.5 V, cheap, shelf-stable) fits, since rechargeability and energy density are wasted there. A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell (2H2 + O2 → 2H2O) is a strong, well-reasoned choice for some EV/grid arguments. Every battery is a galvanic cell (spontaneous redox, E°cell > 0); a secondary cell is recharged by driving the reaction backward (electrolysis). The most common errors: confusing energy density with voltage (a 1.5 V alkaline cell is not “low energy” because of its voltage), treating a primary cell as rechargeable, and inventing specific numbers. Watch for AI-generated arguments with invented voltages or overstated specs — ask the student to verify each figure against the toolkit. Grade from the rubric; keep written comments brief and aimed at the reasoning.

Module 8 — VR Project: Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build — Recorded Walkthrough

This is the capstone of the four-week build and one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 8. The assessed work is the narrated explanation, so coach students to reason aloud — especially the through-line from a spontaneous galvanic cell (anode oxidation/negative, cathode reduction/positive, electrons anode → cathode), through cell potential (E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; Zn–Cu = +1.10 V) and the ΔG° = −nFE° link, to galvanic vs electrolytic, and finally kinetics (Ea, collision theory, a catalyst lowers Ea). Common sticking points: reversing electron flow or the anode/cathode signs (in a galvanic cell the anode is negative; in an electrolytic cell the signs flip but the anode is still oxidation); thinking electrolysis is spontaneous (it is driven, E°cell < 0); claiming a catalyst is consumed or that it changes ΔG, K, or the products (it changes only the rate, by lowering Ea); and reading rate orders off the coefficients (orders are experimental). Demonstrate the OptimaXR video-recording menu/tablet capture, and offer the screen-recording fallback for audio. Finished submissions can be gathered into a teacher-assembled gallery Location for a class walk. Grade from the rubric above; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Module 8 — VR Project Non-VR Alternate: Electrochemical Cell & Rate Build — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)

This alternate produces a narrated video that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The assessed work is the reasoning, not the production quality — coach students to explain why (a galvanic cell runs a spontaneous redox reaction; oxidation is at the anode and reduction at the cathode; electrons flow anode → cathode; E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode and ΔG° = −nFE° link a positive voltage to a spontaneous reaction; electrolysis is driven, not spontaneous; a catalyst lowers Ea without being consumed and without changing the products) rather than just naming parts. Option B's drawn galvanic cell and energy-profile diagram are genuine modeling work and should be encouraged. Common errors: reversing the electron flow or anode/cathode signs, calling electrolysis spontaneous, and claiming a catalyst is consumed or shifts equilibrium. Grade from the same rubric as the VR pathway; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Teacher notes for the Module 9 assignments. Not for students.

Module 9 · Week 1 — VR: Build Your Nuclear Decay & Stability Model

This is the first build of the three-week Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit, so students should leave with placed, locked, signed stations and a saved snapshot. Common sticking points: keeping protons and neutrons visually distinct in the nuclide model, and balancing the decay equations on the panels (watch for the beta-minus “Z + 1” sign and the gamma “no change”). Encourage students to spread the three stations out — they'll add half-life/energy (Week 2) and applications (Week 3) stations to the same bench. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 9 · Week 1 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Build a Nuclear Decay & Stability Model — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” Watch for the most common slips: mixing up protons vs neutrons in the count, forgetting that the band bends upward (more neutrons) for heavy elements, and mis-balancing the beta-minus (Z + 1) and gamma (no change) equations. Encourage students to keep the file tidy; they'll extend it across Weeks 2–3.

Module 9 · Week 2 — VR: Build Your Half-Life & Energy Station

This is Build 2 of the three-week Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit, built on the persistent Nuclear Science Lab Session (spawn Lab Bench A) so work accumulates — students should be continuing from their Nuclear_Wk1_YourName snapshot. Common sticking points: building the decay model as a true halving (some students subtract the same amount each step instead of halving) and labeling the fission/fusion panel clearly. Remind students this is the same shrinking pattern as the Excel decay graph in the hands-on. Encourage them to leave room for Week 3's applications exhibit and final recording. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 9 · Week 2 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Build a Half-Life & Energy Station — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” Common sticking points: building the decay model as a true halving (some students remove the same amount each step instead of halving), and reversing fission/fusion. Remind students this is the same shrinking pattern as the Excel decay graph in the hands-on. Encourage them to keep the file tidy — they'll extend it in Week 3 and record a narrated walkthrough.

Module 9 · Week 3 — VR: Build Your Radioisotope Applications Exhibit

This is the third and final build of the cumulative Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit, so students should leave with a complete, locked, signed exhibit and a saved Nuclear_Final_YourName snapshot — the basis for the module VR project recording. Common sticking points: students writing only the isotope name on a label (push them for radiation type + half-life relevance + use), and crowding the new wing into the older stations (have them clear space first). Remind students that the graded narrated video is the separate module VR project; this week is the build. No live version is needed — support students through this same activity.

Module 9 · Week 3 — VR Non-VR Alternate: Build a Radioisotope Applications Exhibit — No-Headset Pathway

This alternate produces a file that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen,” and it becomes the basis for that student's module VR-project alternate (a recorded walkthrough). Watch for labels that name only the isotope — push for radiation type + half-life relevance + use — and for a cost–benefit note that actually weighs a benefit against a risk rather than just listing one. Encourage students to keep the file tidy and complete; it represents the whole module's work.

Module 9 — Writing Assignment: Marie Curie & the Atom Within: A Nuclear Case Study

This case study is one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 9. There is no single “right” position — reward the accuracy of the history, the quality of the nuclear-chemistry reasoning, and the honesty of the trade-off analysis, not the stance itself. Reference fits: for nuclear energy (A), a strong argument grounds itself in fission (U-235 chain reaction, energy via E = mc2) and/or fusion (D-T, why it's hard) and honestly weighs low-carbon power against waste storage and accident risk; for medical isotopes (B), a strong argument leans on the match of half-life and radiation type to the job (Tc-99m gamma + ~6-hour half-life for imaging; I-131 for the thyroid) and weighs the diagnostic/therapeutic benefit against the radiation dose. The Curie history should hit polonium and radium (1898), radioactivity as a nuclear property that helped retire the indivisible-atom model, and the two Nobel Prizes (1903, 1911). Common errors: confusing fission with fusion, mis-stating the half-life logic ((1/2)n after n half-lives), and either treating a diagnostic dose as catastrophic or treating nuclear power as risk-free — press for an evidence-based middle. As the course capstone, this piece also asks for a hedged current-research connection (with an open question) and an explicit Claim–Evidence–Reasoning conclusion — reward accurate, appropriately tentative claims and flag any that overstate a technology's maturity or invent specifics. Watch for AI-generated text with invented dates, half-lives, or energy figures, or that overstates fusion's maturity — ask the student to verify each claim against the toolkit. Grade from the rubric; keep written comments brief and aimed at the reasoning and the honest weighing of costs.

Module 9 — VR Project: Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit — Recorded Walkthrough

This is the capstone of the three-week build and one of the two teacher-graded items in Module 9. The assessed work is the narrated explanation, so coach students to reason aloud — especially the through-line from an unstable nucleus (nucleons, the band of stability, no stable nuclei past Z = 83) and α/β/γ decay (with A & Z conserved), through half-life (constant t½, (1/2)n remaining, C-14 dating at ≈ 5730 years) and nuclear energy (fission splits, fusion combines, both release energy toward the iron-56 peak via E = mc2), to responsible applications (matching half-life and radiation type to the job; cost/benefit and radiation safety). Common sticking points: confusing fission with fusion (fission splits heavy nuclei, fusion combines light ones); breaking A or Z conservation when balancing a decay equation; thinking half-life changes with sample size or temperature (it doesn't); mis-stating the (1/2)n logic; and treating every dose of radiation as catastrophic or, conversely, treating nuclear technology as risk-free — press for an honest weighing of benefit against risk. Watch for AI-invented half-lives, dates, or energy figures — values should match the course's verified numbers. Demonstrate the OptimaXR video-recording menu/tablet capture, and offer the screen-recording fallback for audio. Finished submissions can be gathered into a teacher-assembled gallery Location for a class walk. Grade from the rubric above; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.

Module 9 — VR Project Non-VR Alternate: Nuclear Decay & Applications Exhibit — Narrated Walkthrough (No-Headset Pathway)

This alternate produces a narrated video that can be gathered into the same class gallery as the VR submissions, so the no-headset student is just as “seen.” The assessed work is the reasoning, not the production quality — coach students to explain why (a nucleus past Z = 83 has no stable form; A and Z are conserved in every decay; half-life is constant and (1/2)n of a sample remains after n half-lives; fission splits and fusion combines, both releasing energy toward the iron-56 peak via E = mc2; an isotope is chosen by matching its half-life and radiation type to the job) rather than just naming parts. Option B's drawn band-of-stability chart, half-life decay sketch, and fission/fusion comparison are genuine modeling work and should be encouraged. Common errors: confusing fission with fusion, breaking A or Z conservation, claiming half-life depends on sample size, and treating a diagnostic dose as catastrophic or nuclear power as risk-free — press for an honest cost/benefit weighing. Grade from the same rubric as the VR pathway; keep written comments brief and focused on the reasoning.
