questions.feedback_general: Pressure = force ÷ area. The same force concentrated onto a smaller area produces a larger pressure.

questions.text: At sea level, the mercury column in a barometer stands at about what height, defining one standard atmosphere?
questions.feedback_general: One standard atmosphere supports a mercury column about 760 mm tall — the basis of the units mmHg and torr.

questions.text: Convert 2.0 atm to millimeters of mercury. (1 atm = 760 mmHg)
questions.feedback_general: 2.0 atm × (760 mmHg / 1 atm) = 1520 mmHg. The atm unit cancels, leaving mmHg.

questions.text: Carrying a barometer up a tall mountain makes the mercury column fall, because there is less air overhead pressing down.
questions.feedback_general: At higher altitude less atmosphere sits above you, so the air pushes less on the dish and the column drops. Lower pressure means a shorter column.

questions.text:
Match each pressure value to the equivalent value in another unit (all equal to one standard atmosphere).

Each value below is equal to 1 atm. Select all values that are equivalent to 1 atm.
questions.feedback_general: One standard atmosphere = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101.3 kPa = 14.7 psi. They are five names for the same sea-level pressure.

questions.text: On the same calm day, two mercury barometers are read: one at a seaside station shows 760 mmHg, and one at a mountain station shows 620 mmHg. What is the best-supported inference?

answers.text: The mountain station is at a higher altitude, where less air sits overhead pressing down.
The seaside station is at a higher altitude than the mountain station.
The air at the mountain station is denser and heavier than the seaside air.
One barometer is broken, because at every location one atmosphere must read exactly 760 mmHg.

questions.feedback_general: A lower barometer reading means less atmosphere is pressing down, which happens at higher altitude — so the 620 mmHg reading points to the mountain station being higher up. (760 mmHg is standard pressure at sea level, not everywhere.)

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.02 — The Gas Laws & the Ideal Gas Law

questions.text: A gas at 1.0 atm fills 2.0 L. At constant temperature, it is compressed to 0.50 L. What is its new pressure? (Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂)
questions.feedback_general: P₂ = (1.0 atm × 2.0 L) / 0.50 L = 4.0 atm. The volume fell to one-quarter, so the pressure rose four-fold.

questions.text: When applying Charles's law or Gay-Lussac's law, the temperature must be in Kelvin, not degrees Celsius.
questions.feedback_general: The gas laws require absolute (Kelvin) temperature. Using Celsius breaks the proportion. Convert with K = °C + 273.

questions.text: In the ideal gas law PV = nRT, what does n represent?

answers.text: The number of moles of gas

questions.feedback_general: n is the amount of gas in moles. (R is the constant, 0.08206; the number of molecules would be n × Avogadro's number.)

questions.text: What volume does 1.00 mol of an ideal gas occupy at STP (273 K, 1 atm)?
questions.feedback_general: V = nRT/P = (1.00 × 0.08206 × 273) / 1.00 = 22.4 L. This molar volume, 22.4 L/mol at STP, is worth memorizing.

questions.text: Match each gas law to the relationship it describes.

answers.right: P and V are inversely related (constant T)
V and Kelvin T are directly related (constant P)
V is directly related to the number of moles (constant T, P)

distractors: P and V are inversely related
V and Kelvin T are directly related
V is directly related to the number of moles
P and V are directly related
questions.feedback_general: Boyle links P and V (inverse); Charles links V and Kelvin T (direct); Avogadro links V and moles (direct). Together with Gay-Lussac they fold into PV = nRT.

questions.text: Boyle's law reliably predicts that halving a gas's volume doubles its pressure, yet the law itself never says why gases do this. Which statement best captures the relationship between a gas law and the kinetic-molecular theory?

answers.text: The gas law describes the measured pattern; the kinetic-molecular theory explains why the pattern happens.
The gas law explains the underlying cause, and the theory merely restates that cause using numbers.
A scientific law and a scientific theory are the same kind of statement with two different names.
Because Boyle's law was discovered first, the kinetic-molecular theory adds nothing and is unnecessary.

questions.feedback_general: A law is an empirical regularity — it faithfully describes what gases do, measured again and again. A theory (here, the kinetic-molecular theory) explains the mechanism behind it: molecules in constant motion striking the container walls. Laws describe; theories explain; both are genuine scientific knowledge.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.03 — Stoichiometry of Gaseous Substances

questions.feedback_general: Equal volumes (same T and P) hold an equal number of molecules, whatever the gas. The masses differ, but the counts are the same.

questions.text: At STP, what volume does one mole of any ideal gas occupy?
questions.feedback_general: The molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (273 K, 1 atm) is 22.4 L/mol — the conversion factor between moles of a gas and its volume.

questions.text: For the reaction 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, all as gases at the same temperature and pressure, how many liters of water vapor form from 5.0 L of O₂ (with H₂ in excess)?
questions.feedback_general: The O₂ : H₂O ratio is 1 : 2, so 5.0 L O₂ × (2 ÷ 1) = 10.0 L H₂O. For gases, the volume ratio equals the mole ratio.

questions.text: Because they have the same volume at the same temperature and pressure, 1 L of helium and 1 L of carbon dioxide have the same mass.
questions.feedback_general: Equal volumes mean equal moles, not equal mass. A mole of CO₂ (44.01 g) is far heavier than a mole of He (4.00 g). Same count, different mass.

questions.text: Match each conversion to the correct factor you would use.

answers.left: Moles of a gas → volume at STP
Moles of reactant → moles of product

questions.feedback_general: Molar mass links mass and moles; molar volume (22.4 L/mol) links moles and gas volume at STP; the balanced equation links moles of one substance to moles of another. Moles are always the hub.

questions.text: At the same temperature and pressure, a 3.0 L sample of methane (CH₄) and a 3.0 L sample of carbon dioxide (CO₂) are found to contain the same number of molecules — even though the CO₂ sample weighs more. Which statement best explains why the counts are equal?

answers.text: The two gases must have the same molar mass.
Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, because a gas is mostly empty space and a molecule's size barely affects how much room it takes up.
The heavier CO₂ molecules pack more loosely, which happens to cancel out the mass difference.
The number of molecules depends only on mass, so equal *masses* would be required for equal counts.

questions.feedback_general: This is Avogadro's law used as reasoning, not recall. Because gas particles are far apart in mostly empty space, molecular size and mass do not change how much volume each particle occupies — so equal volumes (same T, P) mean equal molecule counts, and a volume ratio can stand in for a mole ratio. Mass differs; count does not.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.04 — Gas Mixtures & Dalton's Partial Pressures

answers.text: the average of the partial pressures
the sum of the partial pressures of all the gases
the product of the partial pressures

questions.feedback_general: Each gas exerts its pressure independently, so P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + … — the pressures simply add.

questions.text: A sealed tank holds nitrogen at a partial pressure of 0.60 atm and oxygen at a partial pressure of 0.40 atm, with nothing else inside. What is the total pressure?
questions.feedback_general: Add the partial pressures: 0.60 atm + 0.40 atm = 1.00 atm.

questions.text: In that same tank (total 1.00 atm), what is the mole fraction of nitrogen?
questions.feedback_general: A gas's mole fraction is its share of the pressure: x(N₂) = 0.60 atm ÷ 1.00 atm = 0.60. (And x(O₂) = 0.40, so they sum to 1.)

questions.text: A gas is collected over water at 25 °C, where the vapor pressure of water is 23.8 mmHg. If the total pressure is 760 mmHg, what is the pressure of the dry gas alone?
questions.feedback_general: Subtract the water vapor: P_dry gas = 760 − 23.8 = 736.2 mmHg. The collected gas always carries some water vapor that must be removed from the total.

questions.text: When a gas is collected by bubbling it through water, the gas you collect is pure — no correction to the measured pressure is needed.
questions.feedback_general: The collected gas picks up water vapor, so the measured total includes the water's vapor pressure. You must subtract it to find the dry gas: P_dry gas = P_total − P_water vapor.

questions.text: A student collects hydrogen gas over water at 25 °C and forgets to subtract the water vapor pressure before reporting how much hydrogen was produced. Compared with the true value, the student's reported amount of hydrogen will be:

answers.text: too high, because the water vapor's pressure was counted as if it belonged to the hydrogen
too low, because the water vapor takes pressure away from the hydrogen
exactly right, because water vapor does not contribute to the measured pressure
too low, because some of the hydrogen dissolves into the water

questions.feedback_general: By Dalton's law the measured total is P(dry gas) + P(water vapor). Using the full total as if it were all hydrogen counts the water vapor's 23.8 mmHg as product, overstating the hydrogen. This is why the correction matters for an honest result — you report only the gas you actually made.

quizzes.title: Module 5 Checkpoint — Pressure, Gas Laws, Gas Stoichiometry & Partial Pressures (Lessons 5.01–5.04)

answers.text: The total amount of gas in a container
The temperature of a gas in kelvin
The mass of a gas divided by its volume

questions.feedback_general: Pressure = force ÷ area. A gas exerts pressure because its particles collide with the walls of their container; more frequent or harder collisions over a given area mean higher pressure.

questions.text: A weather report gives the pressure as 2.0 atm. Using 1 atm = 760 mmHg, what is this in mmHg?
questions.feedback_general: 2.0 atm × 760 mmHg/atm = 1520 mmHg. The mercury barometer is why pressure is so often quoted in millimeters of mercury.

questions.text: A gas is measured at 380 mmHg. Expressed in atmospheres, this is:
questions.feedback_general: 380 mmHg ÷ 760 mmHg/atm = 0.50 atm. Half an atmosphere of pressure corresponds to half the standard 760 mm mercury column.

questions.text: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 1.0 atm. It is compressed at constant temperature to 0.50 L. Using Boyle's law (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂), what is the new pressure?
questions.feedback_general: P₂ = P₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = (1.0 atm)(2.0 L) ÷ 0.50 L = 4.0 atm. Boyle's law: at constant temperature, squeezing the volume smaller raises the pressure — P and V are inversely proportional.

questions.text: When using Charles's law or the ideal gas law, temperature must always be expressed in kelvin, not in degrees Celsius.
questions.feedback_general: True. The gas laws are written in terms of absolute temperature. Using Celsius (which can be zero or negative) gives nonsense; convert first with K = °C + 273.

questions.text: A balloon holds 2.0 L of gas at 300 K. Heated to 600 K at constant pressure, what is its new volume (Charles's law, V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂)?
questions.feedback_general: V₂ = V₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁ = 2.0 L × 600 K ÷ 300 K = 4.0 L. Doubling the absolute temperature doubles the volume — V and T are directly proportional (in kelvin).

questions.text: Using PV = nRT with R = 0.08206 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹, what volume does 1.00 mol of an ideal gas occupy at STP (273 K, 1.00 atm)?
questions.feedback_general: V = nRT ÷ P = (1.00)(0.08206)(273) ÷ 1.00 = 22.4 L. This is the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP — one mole of any ideal gas fills 22.4 L at 273 K and 1 atm.

questions.text: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, all gases at the same temperature and pressure, 5.0 L of O₂ reacts completely. By Avogadro's principle (equal volumes hold equal moles, so volume ratios equal mole ratios), what volume of H₂O vapor forms?
questions.feedback_general: The mole ratio O₂ : H₂O is 1 : 2, so the volume ratio is also 1 : 2. 5.0 L O₂ × (2 vol H₂O / 1 vol O₂) = 10.0 L H₂O vapor. For gases at the same T and P, you can reason directly in volumes.
moles CaCO₃ = 10.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.0999 mol → 0.0999 mol CO₂ × 22.4 L/mol = 2.24 L at STP. The path is grams → moles (mole bridge from Module 4) → liters of gas at STP.

questions.text: A container holds nitrogen at a partial pressure of 0.60 atm and oxygen at a partial pressure of 0.40 atm. Match each quantity to its correct value (Dalton's law of partial pressures: P_total = ΣP_i).

answers.left: Partial pressure of a gas collected over water at 25 °C when the total is 760 mmHg

questions.feedback_general: The total pressure is the sum of the partials, 0.60 + 0.40 = 1.00 atm. Each gas's mole fraction equals its partial pressure ÷ total pressure, so N₂ is 0.60 ÷ 1.00 = 0.60. When a gas is collected over water, water vapor (23.8 mmHg at 25 °C) is part of the total, so the dry gas's partial pressure is 760 − 23.8 = 736.2 mmHg.

questions.text: A student compresses a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature and records: Which claim is best supported by these data, and why?

answers.text: Pressure and volume are directly proportional, because both quantities change
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional — each time the volume is halved the pressure doubles, and the product P × V stays constant at 4.0 atm·L (Boyle's law)
There is no relationship between pressure and volume
The data must be in error, because pressure cannot change when volume changes

questions.feedback_general: In every row P × V = 4.0 atm·L (1.0×4.0, 2.0×2.0, 4.0×1.0). A constant product means pressure and volume are inversely proportional — Boyle's law — so halving the volume doubles the pressure. Reading the pattern from the data and stating the reasoning is how an empirical gas law is justified from evidence, not just memorized.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 5.05 — Kinetic-Molecular Theory; Effusion & Diffusion

questions.text: According to the kinetic-molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of the particles in a gas depends on which single quantity?

answers.text: The molar mass of the gas

questions.feedback_general: Postulate 5 of the kinetic-molecular theory: average kinetic energy is set by the absolute temperature alone. That is why all gases at the same temperature share the same average kinetic energy.

questions.text: At the same temperature, a helium atom (4.00 g/mol) moves faster on average than an oxygen molecule (32.00 g/mol).
questions.feedback_general: Same temperature means same average kinetic energy. Since kinetic energy is ½mv², the lighter helium atom must move faster than the heavier oxygen molecule to carry the same energy.

questions.text: What is the difference between diffusion and effusion?

answers.text: Diffusion is the spreading of one gas through another; effusion is gas escaping through a tiny pinhole
Diffusion happens only in liquids; effusion happens only in gases
Diffusion is for heavy gases; effusion is for light gases
They are two words for exactly the same process

questions.feedback_general: Diffusion is one gas mixing through another (perfume crossing a room); effusion is gas particles escaping one at a time through a small hole (a balloon slowly deflating). Both go faster for lighter gases.

questions.text: Using Graham's law, rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁), how many times faster does helium (He, 4.00 g/mol) effuse than oxygen (O₂, 32.00 g/mol)?
questions.feedback_general: rate(He)/rate(O₂) = √(M_O₂ / M_He) = √(32.00/4.00) = √8.00 = 2.83. The lighter gas is faster, so the ratio is greater than 1.

questions.text: Match each gas law to why the kinetic-molecular theory says it happens.

answers.right: Particles reach the walls sooner, so more collisions per second

answers.left: Charles's / Gay-Lussac's law (higher temperature → higher pressure or volume)
answers.right: Faster particles strike the walls harder and more often

answers.left: Dalton's law (total pressure = sum of partial pressures)
answers.right: Particles ignore one another, so each gas pushes as if alone

questions.feedback_general: The kinetic theory explains each measured law with a picture of moving particles — that is what makes it a theory (a mechanism) rather than just a law (a pattern).

questions.text: Boyle measured his pressure–volume law more than a century before anyone could picture moving molecules. Which statement best describes the relationship between Boyle's law and the kinetic-molecular theory?

answers.text: Boyle's law is just an unproven guess that the kinetic-molecular theory later replaced
Boyle's law *describes* a measured pattern; the kinetic-molecular theory *explains why* that pattern happens
The kinetic-molecular theory is less certain than Boyle's law because it is "only a theory"
Boyle's law and the kinetic-molecular theory are two names for the same thing

questions.feedback_general: A law reliably describes what happens (pressure doubles when volume halves); a theory supplies the mechanism that explains why — here, particles reaching the walls sooner when crowded. The theory is not a weaker law waiting to be promoted; it does more work, explaining many laws at once.

questions.text: Under which conditions do real gases deviate most from the ideal gas law, PV = nRT?

answers.text: Low pressure and low temperature only
Real gases never deviate from PV = nRT

questions.feedback_general: High pressure crowds the particles together (their own volume matters) and low temperature lets slow particles feel one another's attractions. These are the conditions near where a gas would condense to a liquid.

questions.text: A gas behaves most like an ideal gas when it is spread out at low pressure and warmed to a high temperature.
questions.feedback_general: Far apart and fast-moving, the particles' finite size and mutual attractions are negligible, so PV = nRT is at its most accurate. The model strains in the opposite corner — high pressure and low temperature.

questions.text: Which two assumptions of the ideal-gas model fail in real gases?

answers.text: That particles move and that they collide
That gases fill their container and that they have mass
That particles have no volume and that they have no attraction for one another
That temperature is measured in kelvins and that pressure is measured in atm

questions.feedback_general: The ideal model treats particles as volumeless points that ignore each other. Real particles do take up space (matters at high pressure) and do attract one another (matters at low temperature).

questions.text: The van der Waals corrections to the ideal gas law do which of the following?

answers.text: Replace PV = nRT with a completely unrelated equation
Add a volume correction (for particle size) and a pressure correction (for attractions)
Apply only to ideal gases, never to real gases
Remove the need to convert temperature to kelvins

questions.feedback_general: Van der Waals kept PV = nRT as the backbone and added a volume correction (the space particles occupy) and a pressure correction (for the attractions). Both fade to nearly zero at low pressure and high temperature, so the equation reduces to the ideal gas law there.

questions.text: The fact that the ideal gas law is "not perfectly true" means it is a bad model that scientists should discard.
questions.feedback_general: False. Every model is a simplification. The ideal gas law is excellent over a huge useful range and even tells you in advance where it will fail (high pressure, low temperature). Knowing a model's limits is part of understanding it — not a reason to throw it away.

questions.text: Two gases are held under identical high-pressure, low-temperature conditions. Gas X is made of large molecules with strong attractions for one another; Gas Y is helium (tiny atoms with very weak attractions). Which gas will deviate more from the ideal gas law, and why?

answers.text: Gas Y, because lighter atoms always move faster and break the ideal assumptions
Gas X, because its larger particle volume and stronger attractions make the two failing assumptions matter more
They deviate equally, because deviation depends only on pressure and temperature, not on the gas
Neither — helium and large molecules both behave perfectly ideally under all conditions

questions.feedback_general: Deviation comes from the two real properties the ideal model ignores: particle volume and intermolecular attraction. Gas X has more of both, so its behavior departs further from PV = nRT. Helium's tiny, weakly-attracting atoms need almost no correction — which is exactly why it stays nearly ideal even when crowded and cooled.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes heat from temperature?

answers.text: Heat and temperature are two words for the same quantity.
Temperature is energy in transit; heat is the average particle motion.
Temperature is the average kinetic energy of particles; heat is energy that flows from a warmer object to a cooler one.
Heat always flows from a cooler object to a warmer one.

questions.feedback_general: Temperature is a property a sample has (average particle motion); heat is energy in transit, always flowing hot → cold until thermal equilibrium.

questions.text: How much heat is needed to warm 50.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C? (c = 4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)
A process that absorbs energy from its surroundings, cooling them down, is endothermic.
questions.feedback_general: Endothermic = energy into the system (surroundings cool). Exothermic = energy out of the system (surroundings warm).

questions.text: In a coffee-cup calorimeter, a hot metal is dropped into cool water. By the first law (conservation of energy), the heat lost by the metal is best described as…

answers.text: equal in size to the heat gained by the water (q_metal = −q_water).
always larger than the heat gained by the water.
unrelated to the water's temperature change.

questions.feedback_general: Energy is conserved: whatever heat leaves the metal (negative q) enters the water (positive q), equal in magnitude — heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water.

questions.text: Match each symbol in q = m·c·ΔT to what it represents.

answers.right: Mass of the sample, in grams

questions.feedback_general: q = m·c·ΔT. Always compute ΔT as final minus initial, and check that grams and degrees cancel, leaving joules.

questions.text: Equal 50.0 g pieces of two different metals, both heated to 100.0 °C, are dropped into identical cups each holding 100.0 g of water at 20.0 °C. Metal X warms its water to a final 28.0 °C; Metal Y warms its water to a final 24.0 °C. Which statement is best supported by this data?

answers.text: Metal Y released more heat to its water than Metal X did.
Metal X has the larger specific heat: for the same mass, it delivered more heat to the water, so by q = m·c·ΔT its c must be greater.
The two metals must have identical specific heats, since the setups were identical.
Conservation of energy was violated in the trial with Metal X.

questions.feedback_general: Both metals cooled from 100 °C by a similar amount, and both masses are equal, so the difference is specific heat. Metal X drove the larger water temperature rise (bigger q_water), so it handed over more energy per gram per degree — the larger specific heat. Energy is conserved in both trials; q_metal = −q_water each time.

questions.text: The enthalpy change (ΔH) of a reaction is best described as…

answers.text: the average kinetic energy of the reactant particles.
the heat released or absorbed by the reaction at constant pressure.
the total mass of the products.

questions.feedback_general: ΔH is the heat of a reaction at constant pressure — the everyday conditions of an open container, which is why a calorimeter can measure it.

questions.text: A reaction has ΔH = −183 kJ. This reaction is…

answers.text: endothermic; it absorbs heat and cools its surroundings.
exothermic; it releases heat and warms its surroundings.
impossible, because ΔH cannot be negative.

questions.feedback_general: A negative ΔH means the reaction releases energy — exothermic. The products sit lower in energy than the reactants, and the surroundings warm up.

It's the reverse. Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic); forming bonds releases energy (exothermic). A reaction is exothermic when forming the product bonds returns more than breaking the reactant bonds cost.

questions.text: Estimate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl using bond energies: H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 243, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol.
questions.feedback_general: Broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH ≈ 679 − 862 = −183 kJ (exothermic).

questions.text: Match each term to its description.

answers.right: ΔH < 0; releases heat; products lower in energy
ΔH > 0; absorbs heat; products higher in energy
Energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond
Estimating a reaction's enthalpy from bond energies

questions.feedback_general: Exothermic = negative ΔH (heat out); endothermic = positive ΔH (heat in); bond energy measures how much energy a bond stores; and you estimate ΔH as bonds broken minus bonds formed.

questions.text: In a certain reaction, breaking all the reactant bonds requires a total of 800 kJ, and forming all the product bonds releases a total of 950 kJ. Without reaching for the specific bonds, what can you conclude?

answers.text: Endothermic, because breaking bonds always outweighs forming them.
Exothermic: forming the product bonds released more (950 kJ) than breaking the reactant bonds cost (800 kJ), so ΔH ≈ 800 − 950 = −150 kJ.
It cannot be classified without knowing which specific bonds are involved.

questions.feedback_general: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = 800 − 950 = −150 kJ. A negative ΔH means the reaction releases energy overall — exothermic — because forming the products returned more energy than breaking the reactants cost. (C flips the sign; A and D ignore the numbers you were given.)

answers.text: Gas molecules attract one another strongly
Gas molecules collide with the walls of the container, exerting force over an area
Gas molecules have large volumes of their own

questions.feedback_general: Pressure is force per unit area, and a gas's pressure comes from countless molecular collisions with the container walls. More frequent or more energetic collisions raise the pressure.

questions.text: Using 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.3 kPa, the pressure 2.0 atm is equal to:
questions.feedback_general: 2.0 atm × 760 mmHg/atm = 1520 mmHg, and 2.0 × 101.3 kPa = 202.6 kPa. All three units describe the same physical pressure.

questions.text: Torricelli's mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column the air can support — at sea level, about 760 mm.
questions.feedback_general: True. Evangelista Torricelli's 1643 barometer is why a standard atmosphere is defined as a 760 mm column of mercury. The atmosphere pushes the mercury up the tube.

questions.text: A gas at 1.0 atm occupies 2.0 L. Compressed at constant temperature to 0.50 L, its pressure becomes (Boyle's law, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂):
questions.feedback_general: P₂ = (1.0)(2.0) ÷ 0.50 = 4.0 atm. Boyle's law: at constant T, pressure and volume are inversely proportional — quarter the volume, quadruple the pressure.

questions.text: A gas at 1.0 atm and 300 K is heated at constant volume to 450 K. Its new pressure (Gay-Lussac's law, P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂) is:
questions.feedback_general: P₂ = P₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁ = 1.0 × 450 ÷ 300 = 1.5 atm. At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute (kelvin) temperature.

questions.text: A rigid sealed canister of gas is left in a hot car, and its temperature climbs. Predict what happens to the pressure inside, and why:

answers.text: Pressure drops, because the molecules slow down
Pressure rises, because the molecules move faster and strike the walls harder and more often
Pressure stays the same, because the volume cannot change
Pressure rises, because the gas gains mass

questions.feedback_general: In a rigid container (constant V), raising the temperature speeds the molecules up, so they hit the walls harder and more frequently — pressure rises with absolute temperature (Gay-Lussac). No mass is added; the molecules just move faster.

questions.text: Using PV = nRT (R = 0.08206), how many moles of gas are in 2.0 L at 1.0 atm and 273 K?
questions.feedback_general: n = PV ÷ RT = (1.0)(2.0) ÷ [(0.08206)(273)] = 2.0 ÷ 22.4 = 0.0893 mol. (Note 2.0 L is one-eleventh of the 22.4 L a full mole would fill at STP.)

questions.text: By Avogadro's principle, equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules — so for reacting gases, volume ratios equal mole ratios.
questions.feedback_general: True. This is what lets you do gas stoichiometry directly in volumes when all gases share the same T and P, without converting to moles first.

questions.text: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (all gases, same T and P), 5.0 L of O₂ produces what volume of H₂O vapor?
questions.feedback_general: O₂ : H₂O is 1 : 2 by moles, hence 1 : 2 by volume. 5.0 L O₂ × 2 = 10.0 L H₂O vapor.
10.0 g ÷ 100.09 g/mol = 0.0999 mol CaCO₃ → 0.0999 mol CO₂ × 22.4 L/mol = 2.24 L at STP. Grams → moles → liters of gas.

questions.text: A container holds N₂ at 0.60 atm and O₂ at 0.40 atm. By Dalton's law, the total pressure is:
questions.feedback_general: P_total = P_N₂ + P_O₂ = 0.60 + 0.40 = 1.00 atm. Each gas contributes its partial pressure independently.

questions.text: A gas is collected over water at 25 °C; the total pressure is 760 mmHg. The water vapor pressure at 25 °C is 23.8 mmHg. The partial pressure of the dry collected gas is:
questions.feedback_general: The collected gas is mixed with water vapor, so P_dry gas = P_total − P_water = 760 − 23.8 = 736.2 mmHg. You must subtract the water vapor's contribution.

questions.text: According to the kinetic-molecular theory, at a given temperature all gases have the same:
questions.feedback_general: Average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature, so all gases at the same T share the same average KE. Because KE = ½mv², lighter molecules must move faster to have the same KE.

questions.text: A gas LAW (such as Boyle's law) is an empirical regularity discovered by measurement, while the kinetic-molecular THEORY is the model that explains why the laws hold.
questions.feedback_general: True. The laws describe what gases do; the theory explains why in terms of moving particles. Distinguishing a measured law from the theory that explains it is part of the nature of science.

questions.text: Using Graham's law (rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁)), compare the effusion of helium (4.00 g/mol) and oxygen (32.00 g/mol):

answers.text: They effuse at the same rate

questions.feedback_general: rate_He / rate_O₂ = √(32.00 ÷ 4.00) = √8 = 2.83. The lighter gas effuses faster; helium escapes through a small opening about 2.83 times faster than oxygen.

questions.text: Real gases deviate most from ideal-gas behavior (PV = nRT) under conditions of:
questions.feedback_general: At high pressure and low temperature, molecules are crowded and slow, so their own volume and their intermolecular attractions — both ignored by the ideal model — matter most. Under those conditions the ideal-gas law breaks down.

questions.text: The ideal-gas model assumes gas particles have no volume of their own and no attractions between them — assumptions that are good approximations only under some conditions.
questions.feedback_general: True. These two simplifying assumptions make PV = nRT work beautifully at ordinary conditions and fail when molecules are crowded together (high P, low T). A model is useful precisely where its assumptions hold.

questions.text: Using q = mcΔT (c_water = 4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹), how much heat is needed to warm 50.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C?
questions.feedback_general: q = (50.0 g)(4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)(80.0 − 20.0 °C) = 50.0 × 4.184 × 60.0 = 12,552 J ≈ 12.6 kJ. Heat scales with mass, specific heat, and the temperature change.

questions.text: A hot metal is dropped into cooler water in an insulated cup and they reach the same final temperature. By conservation of energy (the first law), the heat lost by the metal is:

answers.text: Greater than the heat gained by the water
Equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the heat gained by the water (q_metal = −q_water)
Zero, because the cup absorbs it all
Equal to the temperature of the water

questions.feedback_general: In an ideal calorimeter, energy is conserved: all the heat the metal loses is the heat the water gains, so q_metal = −q_water. The books must balance — that is the first law of thermodynamics applied to calorimetry.

questions.text: For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, estimate ΔH from bond energies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol) using ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed):
questions.feedback_general: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH ≈ 679 − 862 = −183 kJ. A negative ΔH means the reaction releases energy — it is exothermic.

questions.text: A fixed amount of gas is held at constant temperature while its pressure and volume are varied. Plotted as pressure (y) against volume (x), the data form a smooth curve that falls steeply and then levels off, and in every measured pair the product P × V stays constant. Which statement is the best evidence-based interpretation of this graph?

answers.text: Pressure and volume are directly proportional, so the graph is a straight line through the origin
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional (P × V = constant) — this is Boyle's law
Pressure does not depend on volume at all
The gas must be behaving non-ideally

questions.feedback_general: A curve on which the product P × V is constant is the signature of an inverse relationship — Boyle's law. A direct proportion would plot as a straight line through the origin, not a falling curve. Reading the constant-product pattern from the graph is how the law is justified from evidence.

questions.text: A student's coffee-cup calorimetry data give a metal specific heat of 0.383 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹, just below copper's accepted value of 0.385. A classmate claims the slightly low result "proves some energy was destroyed in the cup." Which is the best evidence-based response?

answers.text: The classmate is right — energy was destroyed, so the first law does not apply to real experiments
Energy was conserved; some heat also warmed the cup and escaped to the air, so the water captured slightly less than the metal released — making the calculated specific heat come out a little low
The result is low because the metal cannot be copper
The thermometer added energy to the water, raising the specific heat

questions.feedback_general: Energy is never destroyed (first law). In a real coffee-cup calorimeter some heat leaks to the cup and the surrounding air, so the water gains slightly less than the metal loses. A smaller measured q_water yields a slightly low specific heat — exactly the small gap between 0.383 and the accepted 0.385 for copper. The evidence supports conservation of energy plus real-world heat loss, not the destruction of energy.

questions.text: A fixed amount of gas is held at constant pressure while its temperature (in kelvin) and volume are recorded: Which relationship do these data support, and what is the key reasoning?

answers.text: Volume is inversely proportional to temperature, because both are changing
Volume is directly proportional to absolute (kelvin) temperature — the ratio V/T is constant (0.005 L/K), so doubling the kelvin temperature doubles the volume (Charles's law)
Volume does not depend on temperature
The relationship only holds if temperature is measured in degrees Celsius

questions.feedback_general: In every row V ÷ T = 0.005 L/K (1.0/200, 2.0/400, 3.0/600). A constant ratio means volume and kelvin temperature are directly proportional — Charles's law. Doubling the absolute temperature (200 → 400 K) doubles the volume (1.0 → 2.0 L). The reasoning only works in kelvin; Celsius would give a false ratio.

questions.text: Which intermolecular force is present in every substance, including nonpolar ones?
questions.feedback_general: London dispersion forces arise from the motion of electrons, and every substance has electrons — so every substance has them. In nonpolar substances they are the only intermolecular force acting.

questions.text: Hydrogen bonding occurs only when a hydrogen atom is bonded to one of which three atoms?
questions.feedback_general: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F — small, strongly electron-pulling atoms that leave the hydrogen exposed enough to attract a neighbor's lone pair.

questions.text: For molecules of similar size, which ranking of intermolecular-force strength is correct (weakest → strongest)?

answers.text: They are all equal in strength

questions.feedback_general: For comparable size, London dispersion is weakest, dipole-dipole is stronger, and hydrogen bonding (a strong special case of dipole-dipole) is strongest. Full ionic and covalent bonds are stronger still, but those are bonds, not intermolecular forces.

questions.text: A substance with stronger intermolecular forces will, in general, have a higher boiling point.
questions.feedback_general: Boiling means pulling molecules apart, so stronger forces require more energy and raise the boiling point. This is why you can rank boiling points by reasoning from structure.

questions.text: Match each substance to the strongest intermolecular force acting in it.
questions.feedback_general: Methane is nonpolar (dispersion only); HCl is polar but its H is on chlorine, not N/O/F, so dipole-dipole; water's H is bonded to O, so it hydrogen-bonds — the strongest of the three.

questions.text: Two liquids, X and Y, have nearly the same molar mass. Molecule X is nonpolar; molecule Y contains an –OH group. Which boils at the higher temperature, and why?

answers.text: X, because nonpolar molecules pack together more tightly
Y, because its –OH group allows hydrogen bonding — the strongest of the three intermolecular forces
They boil at the same temperature, because their molar masses match
X, because it has more London dispersion than Y

questions.feedback_general: With nearly equal molar mass, the two have comparable London dispersion, so the deciding factor is the type of force. Y's –OH lets it hydrogen-bond, which X cannot — so Y needs more energy to separate and boils higher. Reasoning from structure (not memorized numbers) gives the answer.

answers.text: pulled inward by their neighbors, with nothing pulling them outward
heavier than the molecules below them

questions.feedback_general: A surface molecule has neighbors below and to the sides but none above, so the net pull is inward — the surface tightens like a skin and the liquid minimizes its surface area.

questions.text: Heating a liquid makes it more viscous (thicker and slower to pour).
questions.feedback_general: False — warming a liquid gives its molecules energy to slip past one another, so viscosity drops as temperature rises. That's why warm honey pours far more easily than cold honey.

questions.text: Water rises in a thin glass tube because…

answers.text: its cohesion is stronger than its adhesion to glass
its adhesion to the glass is stronger than its cohesion
air pushes the water up the tube

questions.feedback_general: Water molecules are strongly attracted to the –OH groups on glass (adhesion), and that adhesion beats the water's cohesion to itself — so the water climbs and forms a concave meniscus.

questions.text: Why does solid ice float on liquid water?

answers.text: Ice is warmer than the water
Air is trapped inside the ice
Hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open lattice, making ice less dense than liquid water
Ice has a higher specific heat

questions.feedback_general: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open, spacious lattice, so solid ice is less dense than liquid water and floats — insulating the water below.

questions.text: Match each of water's special properties to the everyday consequence it explains.

answers.left: Ice less dense than liquid water
answers.right: Lakes don't freeze solid from the bottom up

questions.feedback_general: All three trace back to hydrogen bonding: high specific heat moderates climate, high heat of vaporization makes sweat an effective coolant, and floating ice insulates the water below so lakes stay liquid underneath.

questions.text: Most liquids keep getting denser as they cool right up to freezing. Water is different: it reaches its maximum density near 4 °C and then becomes less dense as it freezes. Which observation is the direct consequence of this anomaly?

answers.text: Ice sinks to the bottom of a pond
Ice forms and floats at the top, insulating the liquid water below
A lake freezes solid from the bottom up
Water cannot exist as a solid at all

questions.feedback_general: Because solid ice is less dense than liquid water, it floats and forms an insulating cap on top. That lets the water underneath stay liquid through winter — so fish and other life survive. (If ice were denser, lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up.)

quizzes.title: Reading Check 6.03 — Phase Transitions & Phase Diagrams

questions.text: Which set of phase transitions all absorb energy (endothermic)?
questions.feedback_general: The transitions toward more freedom — melting (s→l), vaporization (l→g), and sublimation (s→g) — absorb energy to break intermolecular forces. Their reverses release it.

questions.text: On a heating curve, the temperature stays flat (plateaus) during a phase change because the added energy is breaking intermolecular forces rather than raising the molecules' kinetic energy.
questions.feedback_general: During melting or boiling, added energy goes into pulling molecules apart, so the temperature holds constant until the change is complete — the flat step on a heating curve.

questions.text: A liquid boils when…

answers.text: its vapor pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure
all of its hydrogen bonds have broken
the external pressure rises above its vapor pressure

questions.feedback_general: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure rises to equal the external pressure. Lower the external pressure (as at high altitude) and the liquid boils at a lower temperature.

questions.text: On a phase diagram, the triple point is the single set of conditions where…

answers.text: solid, liquid, and gas all coexist in equilibrium

questions.feedback_general: The triple point is where all three phase-boundary lines meet, and solid, liquid, and gas coexist at once. (The point beyond which liquid and gas merge is the critical point.)

questions.text: Match each substance/point to the correct fact from its phase diagram.

answers.right: Slopes left (negative) because ice is less dense
Sublimes straight to gas, no liquid stage
Beyond it, no distinct liquid and gas

distractors: Marks the freezing point at 1 atm
questions.feedback_general: Water's fusion line leans left because ice is less dense than liquid water; CO₂'s triple point is above 1 atm, so dry ice sublimes at ordinary pressure; past the critical point, liquid and gas are no longer distinct.

questions.text: On the phase diagram of water, the solid–liquid (fusion) line leans slightly to the left (a negative slope). A block of ice is held at a temperature just below 0 °C, and then the pressure on it is increased sharply at that constant temperature. Based on the leftward-leaning fusion line, what can happen?

answers.text: Nothing — pressure has no effect on the state of a substance
The ice can melt into liquid water, because raising the pressure crosses the leftward fusion line from the solid region into the liquid region
The ice sublimes directly into gas
The ice stays solid but becomes permanently unable to melt

questions.feedback_general: A leftward (negative) fusion slope means that at a fixed sub-zero temperature, moving up in pressure carries you across the fusion line from solid into liquid — so squeezing ice hard can melt it. That unusual behavior is the phase-diagram fingerprint of ice being less dense than liquid water.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 6.04 — The Solid State & Crystal Lattices

questions.text: A solid has a very high melting point, is extremely hard, and does not conduct electricity. Its whole structure is one continuous web of covalent bonds. Which type of solid is it?
questions.feedback_general: In a covalent-network solid (like diamond or quartz) every atom is bonded into one continuous web, so melting it means breaking actual covalent bonds — giving extreme hardness and a very high melting point.

questions.text: Which property is characteristic of a metallic solid?

answers.text: Conducts electricity only when molten or dissolved
Malleable and conducts electricity as a solid
Hard, brittle, and non-conducting in every state

questions.feedback_general: A metal's cations sit in a sea of delocalized electrons. The mobile electrons let it conduct as a solid, and sliding layers of cations make it malleable and ductile (bends, draws into wire).

questions.text: Why does solid NaCl not conduct electricity, even though it is made of charged ions?

answers.text: Its ions have no charge until it is heated
The ions are locked in the lattice and cannot move; they must be freed by melting or dissolving
Sodium and chlorine cancel each other's charge in the solid
Ionic solids never conduct under any condition

questions.feedback_general: A current needs charges that are free to move. In solid NaCl the ions are pinned in the lattice; only melting or dissolving frees them, so molten or dissolved NaCl conducts but the solid does not.

questions.text: A crystalline solid has a repeating long-range pattern and a sharp melting point, while an amorphous solid like glass lacks that order and softens over a range of temperatures.
questions.feedback_general: Crystalline solids melt sharply because their whole lattice gives way at essentially one temperature; amorphous solids have no long-range order, so they soften gradually instead of melting at a single point.

questions.text: Match each substance to the type of solid it is.
questions.feedback_general: Diamond is one continuous covalent web (network); solid CO₂ is discrete molecules held by weak IMFs (molecular); copper is cations in an electron sea (metallic); NaCl is ions in a lattice (ionic).

questions.text: Two unlabeled solids are tested. Solid X conducts electricity as a solid and can be bent into a new shape without breaking. Solid Y does not conduct as a solid, but its molten form does, and it shatters when struck with a hammer. Which conclusion is best supported by this evidence?

answers.text: X is ionic and Y is metallic
X is metallic and Y is ionic
Both X and Y are covalent-network solids
X is molecular and Y is metallic

questions.feedback_general: Conducting as a solid and bending without breaking is the signature of a metal — a mobile electron sea carries current, and layers of cations slide instead of snapping (so X is metallic). Conducting only when molten, plus shattering when struck, is the signature of an ionic solid — the ions are freed to move only on melting, and the rigid grid of charges splits when a layer is shoved (so Y is ionic).

quizzes.title: Reading Check 6.05 — The Dissolution Process & Electrolytes

questions.text: The rule "like dissolves like" predicts that a solute will dissolve well when:

answers.text: The solute is always denser than the solvent
The solute and solvent have similar polarity (both polar, or both nonpolar)
The solvent is heated to its boiling point
The solute and solvent have opposite polarity

questions.feedback_general: Polar/ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents and nonpolar solutes in nonpolar solvents. Similar polarity means the solute–solvent attractions can compete with the attractions that must be broken.

questions.text: When NaCl dissolves in water, polar water molecules surround the ions and pull them out of the lattice. What is this process called?
questions.feedback_general: Hydration (the general term is solvation) is when solvent molecules surround and cushion each dissolved ion. Water's charged ends form ion–dipole attractions that draw the ions away from the lattice.

questions.text: A strong electrolyte in water:

answers.text: Only partially ionizes, so it conducts weakly
Fully dissociates into ions, so its solution conducts strongly

questions.feedback_general: A strong electrolyte (a soluble salt, strong acid, or strong base) ionizes essentially completely, filling the solution with free ions, so it conducts strongly.

questions.text: Sugar water does not conduct electricity because sugar dissolves as whole, neutral molecules and produces no ions.
questions.feedback_general: Sugar (sucrose) is a nonelectrolyte: it dissolves well but stays as neutral molecules, so no charged particles are free to carry a current and the bulb stays dark.

questions.text: Match each dissolved substance to its electrolyte category.
questions.feedback_general: NaCl, a soluble salt, dissociates completely (strong); acetic acid only partially ionizes (weak); sugar forms no ions at all (none).

questions.text: A student dissolves a different solid in each of two identical glasses of water. Both solids dissolve completely, and the two solutions look exactly the same. A conductivity tester glows brightly in glass 1 but stays dark in glass 2. Which statement is best supported by this evidence?

answers.text: Glass 1 must contain more dissolved solid than glass 2
The solid in glass 1 broke apart into ions, while the solid in glass 2 dissolved as whole, neutral molecules
The water in glass 2 was not polar
The solid in glass 2 did not actually dissolve

questions.feedback_general: A bright bulb means charged particles are free to move, so glass 1's solid must have dissociated into ions (an electrolyte). A dark bulb — even though the solute fully dissolved — means the dissolved particles carry no charge, so glass 2's solid dissolved as whole, neutral molecules (a nonelectrolyte). Both dissolved; only one formed ions. The amount dissolved (A) and the water's polarity (C) are the same in both glasses, and (D) is contradicted by "dissolves completely."

quizzes.title: Module 6 Checkpoint — IMFs, Liquids, Phases, Solids & Solutions (Lessons 6.01–6.05)

questions.text: Which intermolecular force is present in every molecular substance, polar or nonpolar?
questions.feedback_general: London dispersion forces arise from momentary shifts in the electron cloud and act in all substances. Polar molecules add dipole-dipole forces on top; only some can hydrogen-bond.
Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F — small, highly electronegative atoms. This is why water (O–H), ammonia (N–H), and HF have unusually high boiling points.

questions.text: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) boils at 78 °C while ethane (C₂H₆) boils at −89 °C, even though their molar masses are similar. The best explanation is:

answers.text: Ethane is heavier, so it boils lower
Ethanol's –OH group lets its molecules hydrogen-bond, which ethane cannot do
Ethane has stronger London dispersion forces

questions.feedback_general: The –OH (hydroxyl) group lets ethanol form hydrogen bonds; ethane (only London dispersion) cannot. Stronger intermolecular forces take more energy to overcome, raising the boiling point — a functional group setting a physical property.

questions.text: A paper clip can rest on the surface of water because water's strong hydrogen bonding gives it a high surface tension.
questions.feedback_general: True. Surface molecules are pulled inward by cohesion, so the surface resists being broken — high surface tension. Water's hydrogen bonding makes its surface tension among the highest of common liquids.

questions.text: Which special property of water is the reason ice floats on liquid water?

answers.text: Ice is warmer than liquid water
Hydrogen bonds hold solid water in an open structure that is less dense than the liquid
Liquid water is a gas at 0 °C

questions.feedback_general: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open, lattice-like arrangement that takes up more space than liquid water — so ice is less dense and floats. Most substances are denser as solids.

questions.text: A substance changes directly from a solid to a gas without passing through the liquid state. This phase transition is called:
questions.feedback_general: Solid → gas is sublimation (dry ice, solid CO₂, does this at ordinary pressure). The reverse, gas → solid, is deposition.

questions.text: On a heating curve, the temperature stays constant during a phase change (such as melting or boiling) because the added energy is breaking intermolecular forces rather than raising the particles' kinetic energy.
questions.feedback_general: True. During a phase change, added heat goes into overcoming the forces holding particles together, so the temperature plateaus until the change is complete.

questions.text: Match each type of crystalline solid to a property that best characterizes it.

answers.right: High melting point; conducts only when molten or dissolved
Extremely hard; very high melting point
Malleable; conducts electricity as a solid

Extremely hard, very high melting point
Malleable, conducts electricity as a solid
questions.feedback_general: Ionic = held by ion attractions (brittle, conduct when ions can move); molecular = weak IMFs (soft, low-melting); covalent network = a continuous web of covalent bonds (diamond, quartz — extremely hard); metallic = cations in a sea of delocalized electrons (malleable, conductive).

questions.text: A solution conducts electricity strongly. The dissolved solute is most likely a:

answers.text: Strong electrolyte that fully dissociates into ions, such as NaCl

questions.text: Table salt dissolves readily in water but oil does not. The principle that best explains this is:

Salt is a gas at room temperature

questions.text: Three molecules of similar size have the boiling points shown: Which statement best explains this ordering from the intermolecular forces involved?

The maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature
The total mass of a solution

questions.text: A solution holds more dissolved solute than its normal saturation limit, and a single seed crystal makes the excess crash out of solution. This solution is:
questions.feedback_general: A supersaturated solution is "overfull" and unstable — disturbing it (a seed crystal or dust speck) triggers the excess to crystallize. This is how hand-warmers and rock candy work.

questions.text: For most solid solutes, solubility increases as the temperature of the water rises.
questions.feedback_general: Most solids (like KNO₃) dissolve more in hot water than in cold — their solubility curves climb with temperature. A few, like NaCl, are nearly flat.

questions.text: A sealed can of soda fizzes when opened, and warm soda goes flat faster than cold soda. These observations show that the solubility of a gas in a liquid:

answers.text: Increases with pressure and decreases with temperature
Decreases with pressure and increases with temperature
Increases with both pressure and temperature
Does not depend on pressure or temperature

questions.text: A colligative property depends on which of the following?

The number of dissolved solute particles

questions.text: The Tyndall effect — a light beam becoming visible as it passes through — is a way to tell a colloid from a true solution.

answers.left: Milk or fog (cloudy, never settles, scatters light)
Muddy water (particles settle out on standing)

questions.text: Two water solutions are prepared: 1.00 m NaCl (i = 2) and 2.00 m glucose (i = 1). Using ΔTf = i · Kf · m, which solution has the lower freezing point?

Are attractions *between* molecules and are generally much weaker than bonds
Are always stronger than ionic bonds

answers.text: Can form hydrogen bonds (e.g., it contains an –OH group)
Is the lightest of the three

questions.text: Which property of water is directly explained by its hydrogen bonding?

answers.text: Its unusually high specific heat and high surface tension
Its tendency to sink as a solid

questions.text: Match each phase transition to its description.
questions.feedback_general: Melting (s→l) and vaporization (l→g) absorb energy; sublimation (s→g) does too; deposition (g→s) releases it. Freezing and condensation are the other two reverses.

questions.text: A liquid boils when:

answers.text: Its temperature reaches exactly 100 °C in every case
Its vapor pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure
Its density equals that of air

questions.feedback_general: Boiling occurs when a liquid's vapor pressure rises to match the surrounding pressure. Because that external pressure is lower at high altitude, water boils below 100 °C on a mountain.

questions.text: On water's phase diagram, the solid–liquid line slopes slightly to the left (negative slope), which means that increasing the pressure on ice can make it melt — an unusual behavior caused by ice being less dense than liquid water.
questions.feedback_general: True. For most substances the solid–liquid line slopes right; water is the famous exception because its solid is less dense than its liquid, so pressure favors the denser liquid.

questions.text: On a phase diagram, the single point where solid, liquid, and gas all coexist in equilibrium is the:
questions.feedback_general: The triple point is the unique pressure and temperature where all three phases coexist. The critical point, by contrast, is where the distinction between liquid and gas disappears.

questions.text: A solid is very hard, does not conduct electricity, and melts at an extremely high temperature (like diamond or quartz). It is best classified as a:
questions.feedback_general: In a covalent network solid, atoms are joined by a continuous web of covalent bonds (diamond, quartz, silicon carbide). Breaking it means breaking covalent bonds, so it is extremely hard and very high-melting.

questions.text: Solid table salt (NaCl) shatters when struck, but a copper wire bends and dents instead. The best explanation is:

answers.text: In ionic NaCl, a blow shifts ions so like charges align and repel, cracking the crystal; in metallic copper, the electron sea lets cations slide past one another
Salt is a metal and copper is ionic
Copper is held together by hydrogen bonds

questions.feedback_general: Ionic crystals are brittle because displacing the layers brings like charges next to each other, and the repulsion splits the crystal. Metals are malleable because their delocalized electron sea holds the cations together even as they slide — so the metal deforms instead of shattering.

questions.text: When an ionic solid such as NaCl dissolves in water, the ions are pulled from the lattice and surrounded by water molecules. This solute–solvent interaction is:

answers.text: Hydrogen bonding between two Na⁺ ions

questions.feedback_general: Water's polar molecules orient their partial charges toward the ions — ion–dipole attractions (hydration) — and that is what pulls Na⁺ and Cl⁻ out of the lattice into solution.

questions.text: Match each solute to its electrolyte behavior in water.
questions.feedback_general: Soluble ionic salts and strong acids/bases are strong electrolytes; weak acids/bases (like vinegar's acetic acid) partly ionize; molecular compounds like sugar dissolve but form no ions, so they don't conduct.

questions.text: The solubility of most solid solutes in water increases as temperature rises, while the solubility of a gas in water decreases as temperature rises.
questions.feedback_general: True. Heating usually lets more of a solid dissolve (steeper solubility curves), but warm water holds less dissolved gas — which is why warm soda goes flat and warm rivers hold less dissolved oxygen.

questions.text: A solution holds more dissolved solute than its equilibrium solubility, and a single added crystal triggers rapid crystallization. This solution was:
questions.feedback_general: A supersaturated solution holds more than the saturation limit and is unstable; a seed crystal makes the excess solute crystallize out. This is the principle behind some hand-warmers and rock candy.

questions.text: As fresh water grows scarce, the dominant technology for removing dissolved salts from seawater pushes water through a membrane that blocks the ions. This process is:
questions.feedback_general: Reverse osmosis forces water across a semipermeable membrane that holds back dissolved salts, producing fresh water. Distillation (boiling and recondensing) is the other major desalination method.

questions.text: Using ΔT_f = i·K_f·m with K_f(water) = 1.86 °C/m, the freezing point of a 1.00 m NaCl solution (i = 2) is about:
questions.feedback_general: ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C, so the solution freezes at 0 − 3.72 = −3.72 °C. The two ions per formula unit double the depression — which is why salt is spread on icy roads.

questions.text: At the same molality, which solute lowers water's freezing point the most?
questions.feedback_general: Freezing-point depression scales with the van 't Hoff factor i (particles per formula unit). CaCl₂ releases three ions (Ca²⁺ + 2 Cl⁻), the most of the three, so it depresses the freezing point most — useful on the coldest nights.

questions.text: A beam of light shone through a glass of milk reveals a visible path, but the same beam through salt water does not. This difference identifies milk as a:

answers.text: Colloid (it scatters light — the Tyndall effect)

questions.feedback_general: Colloids have particles large enough to scatter light (the Tyndall effect), so the beam's path is visible (milk, fog, gelatin). True solutions like salt water have particles too small to scatter light, so no beam shows.

questions.text: On water's phase diagram, a sample sits just inside the solid (ice) region at a temperature slightly below 0 °C. The pressure is then increased at constant temperature, moving straight up on the diagram. Based on the shape of water's solid–liquid boundary, what happens, and why?

answers.text: Nothing changes, because pressure has no effect on a solid
The ice melts to liquid water, because water's solid–liquid line has a **negative slope**, so higher pressure favors the denser liquid
The ice sublimes directly to vapor, because increased pressure always causes sublimation
The ice simply gets colder and stays solid

questions.feedback_general: Water's solid–liquid line slopes to the left (negative slope) because ice is less dense than liquid water. Increasing the pressure therefore pushes the sample toward the denser phase — liquid — so the ice melts. This pressure-melting behavior is the opposite of most substances, whose solid–liquid line slopes right.

questions.text: Two identical beakers — one holding water, one holding an equal mass of a metal — absorb the same amount of heat. The water's temperature rises far less than the metal's. Separately, a coastal town swings less between day and night temperatures than an inland desert. Which single property, and its molecular cause, best explains both observations?

answers.text: Water's low boiling point, caused by weak intermolecular forces

Water's unusually **high specific heat**, which comes from the energy needed to disrupt its hydrogen bonding — so water absorbs a lot of heat for a small temperature change and moderates the temperature of nearby land
Water's lack of color, which reflects sunlight away
Water's low density as a solid, which is why ice floats

questions.feedback_general: A high specific heat means a large amount of energy raises water's temperature only slightly, because much of that energy goes into disrupting hydrogen bonds rather than speeding up molecules. The same property lets large bodies of water moderate the climate of nearby land — both observations trace back to hydrogen bonding.

questions.text: A solubility table for a solid salt in water is shown: A student dissolves 64 g of the salt in 100 g of water at 60 °C, then slowly cools the solution to 20 °C without disturbing it. Which is the best evidence-based prediction?

answers.text: Nothing was ever dissolved, because the salt is insoluble
At 20 °C only about 32 g can normally stay dissolved, so the cooled solution is now **supersaturated** (holding 64 g); a disturbance or seed crystal could make roughly 32 g crystallize out
Solubility decreases as temperature rises, so heating would have dissolved less
All 64 g will stay dissolved permanently, because cooling always increases solubility

questions.feedback_general: The table shows solubility rising with temperature. Cooling a 64 g/100 g solution to 20 °C — where only ~32 g is normally soluble — leaves it holding more than the limit, i.e. supersaturated and unstable. A seed crystal would crystallize the excess (~32 g). Reading the trend from the data is the evidence for the prediction.

questions.text: For 1.00 m NaCl, the ideal freezing-point depression (van 't Hoff factor i = 2) predicts ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C. A careful measurement gives a slightly smaller depression — as if i were about 1.9 rather than 2.0. Which is the best evidence-based explanation?

answers.text: The measurement must be wrong, because colligative predictions are always exact

In a real solution some Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions briefly **pair up**, so slightly fewer independent particles are present than the ideal count of 2 — the ideal equation is an idealization that real data refine
Water's K_f secretly changes with concentration
NaCl is actually a nonelectrolyte and releases no ions

questions.feedback_general: The value i = 2 assumes every NaCl unit gives two fully independent ions. In real solutions a fraction of ions momentarily pair, so the effective particle count — and the depression — comes out a little below the ideal. This is a model meeting its limits: ideal colligative equations are refined by measured evidence, the honest nature-of-science point behind the numbers.

questions.text: A spontaneous process is best described as one that…

answers.text: always releases heat to the surroundings
can only happen if energy is added the whole time

questions.feedback_general: Spontaneity is about direction, not speed or heat. A spontaneous change proceeds on its own once started — it may be fast or slow, and it may absorb or release heat.

questions.text: Because a reaction is extremely slow, it must be nonspontaneous.
questions.feedback_general: False. Spontaneity tells you the direction nature favors, not the speed. Diamond slowly converting to graphite is spontaneous yet glacially slow. Speed is a separate question (kinetics).

answers.text: how much heat a reaction gives off
the dispersal of energy and matter ("disorder")

questions.feedback_general: Entropy measures how spread out energy and matter are — the number of ways a system can be arranged. It is reported in joules per kelvin (J/K).

questions.text: Which process increases the entropy of the system (ΔS > 0)?

answers.text: Water vapor condensing on a cold window
A solid dissolving and scattering through water
Two moles of gas combining into one mole of gas

questions.feedback_general: Dissolving scatters an ordered crystal's particles throughout the solution — a large increase in disorder. Condensing, freezing, and reducing gas moles all lower entropy.

questions.text: Match each process to the sign of ΔS for the system.
questions.feedback_general: Melting and boiling free particles to more arrangements (ΔS > 0); condensing pulls a gas into a liquid and combining two gas moles into one both reduce arrangements (ΔS < 0). Counting freedom of motion and gas moles predicts the sign.

questions.text: When an instant cold pack is snapped, the salt inside absorbs heat from your hand (the pack turns icy) yet dissolves on its own the moment the pouch breaks. Which statement best explains how an energy-absorbing change can still be spontaneous?

answers.text: The pack must actually be releasing heat; the cold feeling is only an illusion.
Dissolving scatters the salt's ions throughout the water, raising the system's entropy enough to drive the change even though it takes in heat
The change is nonspontaneous and happens only because you physically snapped the pack.
Endothermic changes are always faster than exothermic ones, and that speed forces it to occur.

questions.feedback_general: Spontaneity does not require releasing heat. Here the large increase in the system's entropy (ions dispersing through the solution) outweighs the small entropy loss of the cooled surroundings, so the total entropy still rises and the change runs on its own. Speed is irrelevant to spontaneity.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 7.02 — Second & Third Laws of Thermodynamics

questions.text: The Second Law of Thermodynamics states that for any spontaneous process…

answers.text: the entropy of the system always increases
the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) increases
the entropy of the surroundings always decreases

questions.feedback_general: The Second Law is about the universe: ΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr > 0 for a spontaneous process. The system's own entropy may fall as long as the surroundings gain more.

questions.text: When the entropy of a system decreases, the process cannot be spontaneous.
questions.feedback_general: False. If the surroundings gain enough entropy (usually by absorbing released heat), the total still rises and the change is spontaneous. Water freezing on a cold night is exactly this case.

questions.text: The Third Law of Thermodynamics says that the entropy of a…

answers.text: gas at room temperature is zero
perfect crystal at 0 K is exactly zero
perfect crystal at 25 °C is exactly zero
liquid at its freezing point is zero

questions.feedback_general: A perfect crystal at absolute zero has one motionless, perfectly ordered arrangement — no disorder, so S = 0. This fixed zero gives entropy an absolute scale.

questions.text: Because of the Third Law's true zero point, substances have absolute molar entropies (S°). What is the correct formula for the standard entropy change of a reaction?
questions.feedback_general: ΔS°rxn = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants), with each S° multiplied by its coefficient. Reversing the subtraction would flip the sign of the answer.

questions.text: Match each thermodynamic idea to its correct statement.

answers.right: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K
always a positive value for a real substance above 0 K

questions.feedback_general: The Second Law: total entropy rises for spontaneity; at equilibrium the total change is zero. The Third Law fixes S = 0 at 0 K for a perfect crystal, which makes every real substance's S° a measurable positive value.

questions.text: A student is about to compute ΔS°rxn for 2 H₂O₂(l) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g) from a table of S° values. Before doing any arithmetic, what sign should the answer have, and why?

answers.text: Negative, because two liquid molecules turn into two liquid molecules plus a gas.
Positive, because the reaction produces a gas (O₂) where there was none, a large increase in disorder
Zero, because energy is always conserved in a reaction.
Negative, because gases always have lower entropy than liquids.

questions.feedback_general: The reactant side has no gas; the product side releases a mole of O₂ gas. Producing gas from a liquid is a big jump in the number of arrangements, so ΔS°rxn should be positive — a prediction you can then confirm with the Σproducts − Σreactants calculation. (Energy conservation is a separate law and does not set the sign of ΔS.)

questions.text: Which equation gives the Gibbs free energy change?
questions.feedback_general: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with temperature T in kelvin. The −TΔS term carries the entropy drive: a positive ΔS makes this term negative and favors spontaneity.

questions.text: A reaction has ΔG = −85 kJ at the temperature of interest. What does this tell you?

answers.text: The reaction is nonspontaneous as written
The reaction is spontaneous as written
The reaction cannot occur at any temperature

questions.feedback_general: A negative ΔG means the process releases free energy and is spontaneous (exergonic) — it will proceed forward on its own. ΔG = 0 would mean equilibrium; ΔG > 0 would mean nonspontaneous.

questions.text: A reaction with ΔH < 0 (exothermic) and ΔS > 0 (entropy increases) is spontaneous at all temperatures.
questions.feedback_general: With ΔH negative and ΔS positive, the −TΔS term is also negative, so ΔG is negative no matter the temperature. Both drives agree — nothing can stop it. This is the top row of the four-sign chart.

questions.text: A reaction is endothermic (ΔH > 0) and increases entropy (ΔS > 0). At which temperatures is it spontaneous?
questions.feedback_general: When ΔH and ΔS are both positive, the −TΔS term only beats the positive ΔH once temperature is high enough. So the reaction becomes spontaneous only at high T (ice melting is this case).

questions.text: A problem gives ΔH = −100 kJ, ΔS = +50 J/K, and T = 298 K. What is the most important first step before plugging into ΔG = ΔH − TΔS?

answers.text: Convert ΔS from J/K to kJ/K so the units match ΔH

questions.feedback_general: ΔH is in kJ but ΔS is in J/K — you cannot subtract joules from kilojoules. Convert ΔS to 0.050 kJ/K first. Then TΔS = 298 × 0.050 = 14.9 kJ and ΔG = −100 − 14.9 = −114.9 kJ (spontaneous). Mismatched units are the #1 error on these problems.

questions.text: An endothermic reaction has ΔH = +50 kJ and ΔS = +150 J/K. At T = 400 K, what is the sign of ΔG, and is the reaction spontaneous? (Compute TΔS first.)

answers.text: ΔG is exactly zero; at equilibrium
It cannot be determined without more information

questions.feedback_general: Convert ΔS to 0.150 kJ/K. TΔS = 400 × 0.150 = 60 kJ. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = (+50) − (60) = −10 kJ, which is negative, so the reaction is spontaneous at 400 K. This is the "high-T" case (ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0): raise the temperature enough and the entropy term wins. (Below the crossover T = ΔH/ΔS = 50 / 0.150 ≈ 333 K it would be nonspontaneous.)

quizzes.title: Reading Check 7.04 — Chemical Equilibria & the Equilibrium Constant

questions.text: Which statement best describes a system at dynamic equilibrium?

answers.text: The forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates and concentrations stay constant
The concentrations of reactants and products are always equal to each other
Only the forward reaction is still happening

questions.feedback_general: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations hold steady — but molecules keep converting in both directions. The reaction has not stopped, and reactant and product concentrations need not be equal to each other.

questions.text: For the reaction 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2 SO₃(g), the correct equilibrium-constant expression is:
questions.feedback_general: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient: K = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂]). The coefficients 2, 2, and 1 become the exponents.

questions.text: When writing an equilibrium-constant expression, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted.
questions.feedback_general: Pure solids and pure liquids are left out of K because their concentration doesn't change. Only gases and aqueous (dissolved) species appear. For example, CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) gives K = [CO₂].

questions.text: A reaction has K = 1 × 10⁻⁶. At equilibrium, the mixture contains mostly:

answers.text: Equal amounts of products and reactants

questions.feedback_general: A very small K (much less than 1) means the equilibrium lies far to the left, so very little product forms — the mixture is mostly reactants. A large K (much greater than 1) would mean mostly products.

questions.text: For a reaction with K = 50, you compute the reaction quotient Q = 5 for the current mixture. Which way will the reaction shift?
questions.feedback_general: Q = 5 is less than K = 50, so Q < K — there is too little product. The reaction shifts forward (right) to make more product until Q rises to match K. (Q > K would shift left; Q = K means equilibrium.)

questions.text: For A(g) ⇌ B(g), a flask starts with [A] = 1.00 M and no B. At equilibrium [B] = 0.80 M. Using an ICE table, what is [A] at equilibrium, and is K greater or less than 1?
questions.feedback_general: ICE table — I: [A] = 1.00, [B] = 0; C: −0.80 for A, +0.80 for B; E: [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.80. Then K = [B] ÷ [A] = 0.80 ÷ 0.20 = 4, which is greater than 1, so products are favored. Notice the concentrations are constant but not equal and not zero — both species remain present.

quizzes.title: Module 7 Checkpoint 1 — Spontaneity, Entropy, Free Energy & Equilibrium (Lessons 7.01–7.04)

questions.text: A spontaneous process is best described as one that:

answers.text: Occurs without continuous outside intervention (it may be fast or slow)
Can only happen at high temperature

questions.feedback_general: Spontaneous means the process proceeds on its own once started — it needs no continuous push from outside. It says nothing about speed: rusting is spontaneous but slow, while an explosion is spontaneous and fast.

answers.text: The total energy stored in chemical bonds
The dispersal of energy and matter — informally, "disorder"

questions.feedback_general: Entropy measures how spread out the energy and matter of a system are. More ways to arrange the particles and their energy means higher entropy. Its units are J/K.

questions.text: Which change is expected to show the largest increase in entropy?

answers.text: A gas condensing to a liquid
A liquid freezing to a solid
A solid subliming directly to a gas
A gas being compressed into a smaller volume

questions.feedback_general: Entropy rises in the order solid < liquid < gas. Going straight from an ordered solid to a free-moving gas (sublimation) is the biggest jump in disorder. The other three options all decrease the freedom of the particles.

questions.text: The second law of thermodynamics states that for any spontaneous process the entropy of the universe increases (ΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr > 0).
questions.feedback_general: True. A process can be spontaneous even if the system's own entropy drops — as long as the surroundings gain enough entropy that the total for the universe still rises. At equilibrium, ΔS_univ = 0.

questions.text: The third law of thermodynamics lets chemists assign absolute molar entropies (S°) because it states that:

answers.text: Energy can never be created or destroyed
The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is exactly zero
Heat always flows from cold to hot

questions.feedback_general: The third law fixes a true zero on the entropy scale: a perfect, motionless crystal at absolute zero has S = 0. From that anchor, every substance has a measurable absolute entropy S° (in J/mol·K).

questions.text: The Gibbs free energy change is calculated as:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with the temperature T in kelvin. This single equation combines the enthalpy and entropy changes to tell you whether a process is spontaneous.
