questions.text: For a reaction at 298 K, ΔH = −100 kJ and ΔS = +50 J/K (= +0.050 kJ/K). What is ΔG, and is the reaction spontaneous?
questions.feedback_general: TΔS = 298 × 0.050 = 14.9 kJ, so ΔG = −100 − 14.9 = −114.9 kJ. A negative ΔG means the reaction is spontaneous (exergonic). Here both a negative ΔH and a positive ΔS push the same way, so it is spontaneous at all temperatures.

questions.text: Match each combination of signs to whether the reaction is spontaneous. (T in kelvin.)
questions.feedback_general: In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the −TΔS term grows with temperature. When ΔH and ΔS push the same way (−/+ or +/−), temperature can't change the outcome. When they conflict (−/− or +/+), temperature decides — low T favors the enthalpy term, high T favors the entropy term.

questions.text: A reaction is at dynamic equilibrium when:

answers.text: All reactants have been used up
The forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant

questions.feedback_general: At dynamic equilibrium the reaction has not stopped — the forward and reverse reactions are both still happening, but at equal rates, so the macroscopic concentrations no longer change. It requires a closed system.

questions.text: For the reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant has a value K = 1 × 10⁶ (much greater than 1). This tells you that at equilibrium:

answers.text: The mixture is exactly 50% reactants and 50% products
The reaction is not at equilibrium

questions.feedback_general: K = [products]^coeffs / [reactants]^coeffs. A large K (≫ 1) means the numerator dominates — products are favored. A small K (≪ 1) would mean reactants are favored. Pure solids and liquids are left out of the K expression.

questions.text: A reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +30 kJ) and increases the system's entropy (ΔS = +100 J/K). Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, at which temperatures is the reaction spontaneous?

answers.text: Only at high temperatures — once the −TΔS term outweighs the positive ΔH

questions.feedback_general: With ΔH positive and ΔS positive, the two terms conflict. At low T the −TΔS term is too small, so ΔG > 0 (nonspontaneous); as T rises, −TΔS grows until it overcomes the positive ΔH and ΔG turns negative. The reaction "switches on" — it becomes spontaneous only above a threshold temperature. (Contrast the −/+ case, which is spontaneous at every temperature.)

questions.text: According to Le Châtelier's principle, when a system at equilibrium is stressed, it shifts in the direction that:
questions.feedback_general: A stressed equilibrium shifts to partially counteract the change — it moves part-way toward a new equilibrium, never fully undoing what you did.

questions.text: For the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), adding more H₂ (a reactant) will shift the equilibrium:

answers.text: to the left, toward N₂ and H₂

questions.feedback_general: Adding a reactant is a stress the system relieves by consuming some of it — it shifts right (toward products), making more NH₃.

questions.text: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (4 moles of gas on the left, 2 on the right), increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium:

answers.text: to the right, toward the side with fewer moles of gas
to the left, toward the side with more moles of gas
in neither direction, because pressure never affects equilibrium
only if a catalyst is also added

questions.feedback_general: Increasing pressure shifts a gas equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles — here the right side (2 mol), favoring more NH₃.

questions.text: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
questions.feedback_general: False. A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster. It does not shift the position or change how much product forms.

questions.text: The Haber reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol). Treating heat as a product, raising the temperature will:

answers.text: shift the equilibrium right, toward more ammonia
shift the equilibrium left, away from ammonia
have no effect on the equilibrium

questions.feedback_general: Because the reaction is exothermic, heat is a product. Adding heat (raising T) shifts the equilibrium left, away from ammonia — which is why industry compromises on a moderate temperature instead of just lowering it.

questions.text: For the exothermic equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (4 mol gas on the left, 2 mol on the right, heat is a product), match each stress to the direction the equilibrium shifts.
questions.feedback_general: Each stress is judged on its own: add a substance → shift away from it; remove one → shift toward it; higher pressure → toward fewer gas moles; for this exothermic reaction heat is a product, so raising T shifts left; a catalyst never moves the position.

questions.text: In an ICE table, what do the three letters stand for?
questions.feedback_general: I = Initial concentrations, C = Change as the system reaches equilibrium, E = Equilibrium concentrations (Initial + Change).

questions.text: For the reaction A + 3B ⇌ 2C, if x represents how much A reacts, the "Change" row should be written as:
questions.feedback_general: The Change row uses the balanced coefficients: A loses x, B loses 3x (coefficient 3), and C gains 2x (coefficient 2). Reactants get minus signs, products get plus signs.

questions.text: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), a flask starts with 1.00 M H₂ and 1.00 M I₂. At equilibrium [HI] = 1.60 M. Since [HI] = 2x, what is x, and what is the equilibrium [H₂]?
Using the equilibrium concentrations [H₂] = 0.20 M, [I₂] = 0.20 M, and [HI] = 1.60 M, what is Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂])?
questions.feedback_general: Kc = (1.60)² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 / 0.04 = 64. A K well above 1 means products are favored.

questions.text: When K is very small, the change x is tiny compared with the initial concentration, so a term like "1.00 − x" can be approximated as "1.00."
questions.feedback_general: True. A very small K means very little reactant converts, so x is negligible and the small-x approximation lets you avoid a messy quadratic.

questions.text: A flask starts with 1.00 M N₂O₄ and no NO₂ for the reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). The Equilibrium row of the ICE table reads [N₂O₄] = 1.00 − x and [NO₂] = 2x. If you measure [NO₂] = 0.60 M at equilibrium, what is the equilibrium [N₂O₄]?
questions.feedback_general: Read the row: [NO₂] = 2x = 0.60, so x = 0.30. Then [N₂O₄] = 1.00 − x = 1.00 − 0.30 = 0.70 M. (Notice the coefficient 2 means x is half the measured [NO₂], not equal to it.)

questions.text: In the Brønsted-Lowry model, an acid is defined as a substance that…
questions.feedback_general: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor; a base is a proton acceptor. This is broader than the Arrhenius model and does not depend on water.

questions.text: The two members of a conjugate acid-base pair always differ by…
questions.feedback_general: Conjugate partners differ by exactly one H⁺. For example, HCl/Cl⁻ and H₂O/H₃O⁺ each differ by a single proton.

questions.text: Water is described as amphoteric because it can…

answers.text: act as either a proton donor or a proton acceptor

questions.feedback_general: Water donates a proton to ammonia (acting as an acid) and accepts one from HCl (acting as a base) — it can play either role.

questions.text: The autoionization of water is written 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, with K𝓌 = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
questions.feedback_general: In pure water, one molecule donates a proton and another accepts it, giving H₃O⁺ and OH⁻. Their product, K𝓌, is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.

questions.text: Match each species to its conjugate partner (differing by one H⁺).
questions.feedback_general: Remove one H⁺ from an acid to get its conjugate base (HNO₃ → NO₃⁻); add one H⁺ to a base to get its conjugate acid (NH₃ → NH₄⁺; OH⁻ → H₂O).

questions.text: Ammonia (NH₃) acts as a base in water even though it contains no OH⁻ to release. Which acid-base model is needed to explain this, and why?

answers.text: The Arrhenius model, because ammonia produces OH⁻ directly
The Brønsted-Lowry model, because ammonia **accepts** a proton (H⁺) from water
The Arrhenius model, because ammonia is dissolved in water
No model is needed; ammonia is not really a base

questions.feedback_general: The Arrhenius model requires a base to supply OH⁻, which ammonia cannot do — so it fails here. The Brønsted-Lowry model explains it: NH₃ accepts a proton from water (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻), making it a proton acceptor, i.e., a base. This case is exactly why the definition had to broaden.

questions.text: The pH of a solution is defined as…
questions.feedback_general: pH = −log[H₃O⁺]. The negative sign makes the value positive for ordinary solutions, and lower pH means more hydronium (more acidic).

questions.text: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. Its pH is…
questions.feedback_general: pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.00. Since 3.00 is below 7, the solution is acidic.

questions.text: At 25 °C, which statement is always true?
questions.feedback_general: Because [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = K𝓌 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, taking −log of both sides gives pH + pOH = 14.00.

questions.text: A solution has pH = 9.00 at 25 °C. The solution is… and its [H₃O⁺] is…
questions.feedback_general: pH 9.00 is above 7, so the solution is basic. Recover concentration with [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻pH = 10⁻⁹ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ M. (Its pOH = 5.00, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁵ M.)

questions.text: A solution with pH = 2 is more acidic than a solution with pH = 5.
questions.feedback_general: Lower pH means more hydronium and greater acidity. Each pH unit is a factor of ten, so pH 2 has 1,000 times the hydronium of pH 5.

questions.text: A solution has [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M at 25 °C. What is its pH, and is it acidic or basic?
questions.feedback_general: First find pOH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 4.00. Then use pH + pOH = 14.00, so pH = 14.00 − 4.00 = 10.00. Because pH is above 7, the solution is basic. (Two steps: get pOH from [OH⁻], then convert to pH.)

quizzes.title: Reading Check 7.09 — Relative Strengths of Acids & Bases

questions.text: A strong acid is one that…
questions.feedback_general: "Strong" describes how completely an acid ionizes — nearly 100% — not how concentrated it is. A weak acid ionizes only partially.

questions.text: Which of the following is a weak acid?
questions.feedback_general: HCl, HNO₃, and HClO₄ are on the short list of strong acids. Acetic acid (Ka ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) ionizes only partially, so it is weak.

questions.text: Acid X has Ka = 1 × 10⁻³ and Acid Y has Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁷. Which is the stronger acid?
questions.feedback_general: A larger Ka means the ionization lies further toward products — more protons donated. Since 10⁻³ > 10⁻⁷, Acid X is stronger. (Equivalently, X has the smaller pKa.)

questions.text: The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
questions.feedback_general: The seesaw rule: an acid that donates protons eagerly leaves behind a conjugate base with little tendency to take a proton back. HCl (strong) has the very weak conjugate base Cl⁻.

questions.text: Match each species to its classification.
questions.feedback_general: HBr is on the strong-acid list; NaOH is a group-1 hydroxide (strong base); ammonia accepts protons only partially and is not a metal hydroxide, so it is a weak base.

questions.text: Three acids have the following data: Acid J, Ka = 1 × 10⁻²; Acid K, pKa = 4.7; Acid L, Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁹. Ranked from strongest to weakest acid, the order is…
questions.feedback_general: Put them on one scale. Larger Ka = stronger, and smaller pKa = stronger. Acid J (Ka = 10⁻², so pKa = 2.0) is strongest; Acid K (pKa = 4.7, i.e. Ka ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵) is in the middle; Acid L (Ka = 10⁻⁹, pKa = 9.0) is weakest. So J > K > L.

quizzes.title: Module 7 Checkpoint 2 — Le Châtelier, ICE Tables & Acid-Base Foundations (Lessons 7.05–7.09)

answers.text: Shifting to partially counteract the stress
Changing the value of K only

questions.feedback_general: When a stress (added/removed substance, pressure or volume change, temperature change) disturbs an equilibrium, the system shifts in the direction that partially offsets the change and restores balance.

questions.text: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), adding more N₂ to the system at equilibrium will cause the equilibrium to:
questions.feedback_general: Adding a reactant stresses the left side, so the system shifts right to consume the added N₂ and make more product (NH₃). Adding a product, or removing a reactant, would push the other way.

questions.text: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol). To maximize the yield of NH₃, which conditions favor the products?
questions.feedback_general: High pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles (4 mol of gas → 2 mol), favoring NH₃. Because the reaction is exothermic, low temperature also favors product. (Industry compromises on a moderate temperature with a catalyst, since low temperature alone makes the reaction too slow.)

questions.text: In an ICE table, the three rows stand for:
questions.feedback_general: ICE = Initial concentrations, the Change (written using the stoichiometric coefficients, with ±x), and the Equilibrium concentrations. It is the bookkeeping tool for solving equilibrium problems.

questions.text: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), a system starts with 1.00 M H₂ and 1.00 M I₂. At equilibrium 1.60 M HI has formed, so [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.20 M. What is Kc?
questions.feedback_general: Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = (1.60)² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 / 0.04 = 64. The +2x change in HI comes from the coefficient of 2 in the balanced equation.

questions.text: According to the Brønsted-Lowry definitions, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. In the reaction NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, water acts as the:

answers.text: Brønsted-Lowry acid (it donates a proton to NH₃)

questions.feedback_general: Here water donates an H⁺ to ammonia, so water is the Brønsted-Lowry acid and NH₃ is the base. Water is amphoteric — it can act as an acid or a base depending on its partner.

questions.text: Which pair is a correct conjugate acid-base pair (differing by exactly one H⁺)?
questions.feedback_general: A conjugate pair differs by one proton: NH₄⁺ (acid) loses an H⁺ to become NH₃ (its conjugate base). Other valid pairs include HCl/Cl⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O.

questions.text: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. What is its pH, and is it acidic or basic?
questions.feedback_general: pH = −log[H₃O⁺] = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.00. A pH below 7 is acidic (at 25 °C). Its pOH would be 14.00 − 3.00 = 11.00.

questions.text: At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.00, because the autoionization of water gives Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
questions.feedback_general: True. Taking the negative log of Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ gives pH + pOH = 14.00 at 25 °C. So if you know one, you can always find the other.

questions.text: Match each substance to its acid-base strength classification.
questions.feedback_general: Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄) and strong bases (group-1 hydroxides, plus Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂) ionize essentially completely. Weak acids/bases ionize only partially and are described by Ka/Kb — a larger Ka means a stronger acid. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

questions.text: The reaction N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) is endothermic (ΔH = +57 kJ/mol). If the temperature of the system is increased, the equilibrium will:

answers.text: Shift right, toward NO₂, because for an endothermic reaction heat behaves like a reactant
Not shift; temperature has no effect

questions.feedback_general: For an endothermic reaction, heat is effectively a reactant; adding heat (raising T) pushes the equilibrium toward products (more NO₂) and raises K. This is the mirror image of the exothermic Haber case in Q3, where raising the temperature lowers the NH₃ yield — so the temperature rule depends on the sign of ΔH.

questions.text: A salt formed from a strong acid and a strong base (such as NaCl) produces a solution that is:
questions.feedback_general: Both ions (e.g., Na⁺ and Cl⁻) are conjugates of a strong base and a strong acid, so they are spectators that do not react with water. With nothing to shift the pH, the solution stays neutral.

questions.text: Which ion is responsible for making a solution of sodium acetate (NaC₂H₃O₂) slightly basic?
questions.feedback_general: Acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid (acetic acid), so it hydrolyzes — pulling a proton off water and leaving OH⁻ behind, which makes the solution basic. Na⁺ is just a spectator.

questions.text: A solution of ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) is acidic because:

answers.text: NH₄⁺ donates a proton to water, producing H₃O⁺
NH₄Cl is itself a strong acid

questions.feedback_general: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base ammonia, so it donates a proton to water and produces extra H₃O⁺, making the solution acidic. Cl⁻ (from strong acid HCl) is a spectator.

questions.text: Only the ion that is the conjugate of a weak acid or weak base reacts with water; conjugates of strong acids or strong bases act as spectators.
questions.feedback_general: Because a strong acid/base has a negligibly weak conjugate, those ions don't react with water. Only conjugates of weak acids/bases are reactive enough to hydrolyze and shift the pH.

questions.text: Match each salt to the character of its solution.
questions.feedback_general: KNO₃ has two spectator ions → neutral. Sodium acetate's anion is the conjugate of a weak acid → basic. Ammonium chloride's cation is the conjugate of a weak base → acidic.

questions.text: You are handed a salt you did not study in the lesson: potassium fluoride (KF), formed from the strong base KOH and the weak acid HF (hydrofluoric acid). Predict the character of its solution.

answers.text: neutral, because both K⁺ and F⁻ are always spectators

questions.feedback_general: Trace it: K⁺ comes from the strong base KOH, so it is a spectator. F⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HF, so it hydrolyzes — pulling a proton off water and leaving OH⁻ behind. Strong base + weak acid → basic. (This is the same reasoning as sodium acetate, applied to a salt you had never seen.)

questions.text: A buffer is best described as a solution containing:

answers.text: a strong acid and a strong base
a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid)
a salt of two strong parents

questions.feedback_general: A buffer pairs a weak acid with its conjugate base (or a weak base with its conjugate acid). One partner absorbs added acid and the other absorbs added base, so the pH barely changes.

questions.text: According to the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻]/[HA]), what is the pH of a buffer in which [A⁻] = [HA]?
questions.feedback_general: When [A⁻] = [HA], the ratio is 1 and log(1) = 0, so pH = pKₐ. A half-and-half buffer always sits right at the weak acid's pKₐ.

questions.text: For a polyprotic acid, the successive ionization constants follow the order Kₐ1 > Kₐ2 > Kₐ3.
questions.feedback_general: Each proton is pulled off an increasingly negative ion, which holds the remaining protons more tightly, so each step is harder than the last: Kₐ1 > Kₐ2 > Kₐ3.

questions.text: Which weak-acid / conjugate-base pair is the main buffer that keeps human blood near pH 7.4?
questions.feedback_general: The carbonic-acid / bicarbonate pair (H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻), drawn from diprotic carbonic acid, buffers the blood near pH 7.4 — and the same pair buffers the ocean.

questions.text: Which of the following is a triprotic acid (donates three protons in successive steps)?
questions.feedback_general: Phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄, has three ionizable hydrogens, so it is triprotic. H₂SO₄ and H₂CO₃ are diprotic (two protons); HCl and acetic acid are monoprotic.

questions.text: Two acetate buffers are each mixed half-and-half, so both start at the same pH (pH = pKₐ = 4.74). Buffer X is 1.0 M in acetic acid and 1.0 M in acetate; Buffer Y is 0.010 M in each. You add the same large squirt of strong acid to each. Which buffer holds its pH better, and why?

answers.text: Buffer Y, because it is more dilute and dilution always resists change
Buffer X, because it holds a larger reservoir of both partners, giving it greater buffer capacity
Neither — since they start at the same pH, they must resist change equally
Buffer X, because a higher concentration raises the pKₐ

questions.feedback_general: Both buffers begin at pH 4.74 because pH depends on the ratio [A⁻]/[HA], which is 1 in both. But capacity depends on how much of each partner is actually present. Buffer X has 100× more acetic acid and acetate on hand, so it can neutralize far more added acid before a partner runs out. Starting pH is set by the ratio; capacity is set by the amounts.

questions.text: At the equivalence point of a titration:

answers.text: the indicator has not yet changed color
the moles of added titrant exactly equal the moles of the substance being titrated
the pH is always exactly 7, no matter what

questions.feedback_general: The equivalence point is the stoichiometric meeting point — moles of added base equal moles of acid (or vice versa). The pH there depends on the salt formed, so it is not always 7.

questions.text: It takes 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH to titrate 25.0 mL of HCl to the equivalence point. What is the concentration of the HCl?
The equivalence-point pH for a weak acid titrated with a strong base is:
questions.feedback_general: The salt formed has an anion that is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it hydrolyzes and leaves the solution basic — the equivalence point lands above pH 7.

questions.text: On a titration curve (pH vs. volume of titrant), the equivalence point lies within the steep, nearly vertical region of the curve.
questions.feedback_general: Near the equivalence point so little acid (or base) remains that a single drop of titrant changes the pH by several units, producing the steep vertical jump that brackets the equivalence point.

questions.text: Phenolphthalein, a common acid-base indicator, is:

answers.text: pink in acid and colorless in base
colorless in acid and pink in base (changing around pH 8.2–10)

questions.feedback_general: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic solution and turns pink in basic solution, switching around pH 8.2–10. Its color change near the equivalence point signals when to stop adding titrant.

questions.text: You record a titration curve for an unknown acid titrated with a strong base. The curve rises gently, then jumps steeply, and the middle of the steep region is centered at about pH 9 (well above 7). What does the position of that steep region tell you about the acid?

answers.text: The acid must be a strong acid
The acid is a weak acid, since its equivalence point lands above pH 7
The buret was read incorrectly; a steep region can only cross pH 7
Nothing — the center of the steep region is unrelated to the acid's strength

questions.feedback_general: For a strong acid + strong base the equivalence point sits at pH 7. When the steep region centers above 7, the salt formed must be basic — its anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid that hydrolyzes (Lesson 7.10). So a high equivalence-point pH is direct evidence that the acid being titrated is weak. (Phenolphthalein, changing near pH 8.2–10, is a good indicator here.)

quizzes.title: Module 7 Exam — Thermodynamics, Equilibrium & Acid-Base Chemistry (Lessons 7.01–7.12)

questions.text: A process is spontaneous if it:

answers.text: Occurs without continuous outside intervention, whether fast or slow
Always absorbs heat from the surroundings

questions.feedback_general: Spontaneity is about direction, not speed. A spontaneous process proceeds on its own once underway — rusting (slow) and combustion (fast) are both spontaneous.

questions.text: Which process is expected to increase the entropy of the system?

answers.text: Water vapor condensing on a window
A solid dissolving to form a solution
A gas being cooled and compressed

questions.feedback_general: Dissolving disperses particles and energy, raising entropy. Condensing, compressing/cooling a gas, and freezing all reduce particle freedom and lower entropy. Entropy rises in the order solid < liquid < gas, and reactions that make more gas moles raise it too.

questions.text: The second law of thermodynamics says that for any spontaneous process the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) increases.
questions.feedback_general: True. ΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr > 0 for a spontaneous change. The system's own entropy may decrease, provided the surroundings gain even more. At equilibrium, ΔS_univ = 0.

questions.text: The third law of thermodynamics makes it possible to tabulate absolute molar entropies (S°) because it sets which reference point?

answers.text: The entropy of a gas at 1 atm is zero
The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is exactly zero
The entropy of water at 25 °C is zero
The entropy of any element is zero

questions.feedback_general: The third law fixes a true zero: a perfect, motionless crystal at absolute zero has S = 0. From that anchor, each substance has a measurable absolute entropy S° (J/mol·K), so ΔS°_rxn = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants).

questions.text: The Gibbs free energy change is given by:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin) combines enthalpy and entropy into a single spontaneity criterion: ΔG < 0 is spontaneous, ΔG > 0 is nonspontaneous, ΔG = 0 is at equilibrium.

questions.text: For a reaction at 298 K with ΔH = −100 kJ and ΔS = +50 J/K (+0.050 kJ/K), the value of ΔG is:
questions.feedback_general: TΔS = 298 × 0.050 = 14.9 kJ, so ΔG = −100 − 14.9 = −114.9 kJ. The negative value means the reaction is spontaneous. Watch the unit conversion: ΔS in J/K must become kJ/K to subtract from ΔH in kJ.

questions.text: Match each sign combination to its temperature dependence for spontaneity.
questions.feedback_general: When ΔH and ΔS push the same direction (−/+ or +/−), temperature can't change the outcome. When they conflict (−/− or +/+), the −TΔS term decides: low T favors enthalpy, high T favors entropy.

questions.text: A reaction has ΔH = +50 kJ (endothermic) and ΔS = +120 J/K (entropy increases). This reaction is best described as:

answers.text: Nonspontaneous at low temperature but spontaneous at high temperature

questions.feedback_general: With ΔH positive and ΔS positive, the two terms conflict. At low T the −TΔS term is small, so ΔG > 0 (nonspontaneous); raising T makes −TΔS large and negative enough to overcome ΔH, flipping ΔG negative. The reaction "turns on" above a threshold temperature.

questions.text: A reaction at dynamic equilibrium is one in which:

answers.text: The forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant
The reactants are entirely converted to products

questions.feedback_general: At dynamic equilibrium both directions are still occurring, at equal rates, so the visible concentrations hold steady. Equilibrium requires a closed system; the reaction never truly stops.

questions.text: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, which statement about the equilibrium constant K is correct?

answers.text: Pure solids and liquids are included in the K expression
K = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b), and a large K means products are favored
K changes whenever a catalyst is added

questions.feedback_general: K is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient; pure solids and liquids are omitted. A large K (≫ 1) favors products, a small K (≪ 1) favors reactants. A catalyst does not change K.

questions.text: The reaction quotient Q is compared to K to predict direction. If Q < K, the reaction will:
questions.feedback_general: Q < K means there is too little product relative to equilibrium, so the reaction shifts forward (right) to make more product. Q > K shifts left; Q = K means it is already at equilibrium.

questions.text: For an equilibrium of gases, increasing the pressure (by decreasing the volume) shifts the system toward:

answers.text: The side with more moles of gas
The side with fewer moles of gas
The side with the heavier molecules
Neither side; pressure has no effect

questions.feedback_general: Compressing the system raises the pressure; the equilibrium shifts toward whichever side has fewer gas molecules, which relieves the pressure. If both sides have equal gas moles, a pressure change causes no shift.

questions.text: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol). Which set of conditions would, by Le Châtelier's principle alone, maximize the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
questions.feedback_general: High pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles (4 mol → 2 mol of NH₃). Because the reaction releases heat, low temperature also shifts toward product (treat heat as a product). In practice industry uses a moderate temperature plus an iron catalyst, since very low temperature makes the reaction far too slow — a real-world compromise between yield and rate.

questions.text: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
questions.feedback_general: False. A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the system reaches equilibrium faster but the position of equilibrium (and K) is unchanged.

questions.text: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), a mixture begins at 1.00 M H₂ and 1.00 M I₂; at equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.20 M and [HI] = 1.60 M. The value of Kc is:
questions.feedback_general: Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = (1.60)² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 / 0.04 = 64. The change in HI is +2x because of the coefficient 2 in the balanced equation.

questions.text: In an ICE table for aA ⇌ products, the "C" (Change) row entries are written using:

answers.text: The stoichiometric coefficients, as multiples of x (e.g., −x, +2x)

questions.feedback_general: The Change row uses the balanced coefficients with the unknown x: reactants decrease (−x, −2x, …) and products increase (+x, +2x, …) in proportion to their coefficients. Adding Initial + Change gives the Equilibrium row.

questions.text: Under the Brønsted-Lowry definitions, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, the base is:
questions.feedback_general: Water accepts the proton donated by HCl, so water is the Brønsted-Lowry base here and HCl is the acid. Water is amphoteric — it can donate or accept a proton depending on its partner.

questions.text: Which is a correct conjugate acid-base pair, differing by exactly one H⁺?
questions.feedback_general: A conjugate pair differs by a single proton: H₃O⁺ loses one H⁺ to become H₂O. (H₂SO₄/SO₄²⁻ differ by two protons; HCl/NaOH are not a conjugate pair.)

questions.text: The autoionization of water, 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, has an equilibrium constant Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
questions.feedback_general: True. In pure water at 25 °C, [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M, so their product Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. This constant links [H₃O⁺] and [OH⁻] in every aqueous solution.

questions.text: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. Its pH, and whether it is acidic or basic, is:
questions.feedback_general: pH = −log[H₃O⁺] = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.00. A pH below 7 (at 25 °C) is acidic. The pOH would be 14.00 − 3.00 = 11.00, giving [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ M.

questions.text: Which group lists only strong acids (those that ionize essentially 100% in water)?
questions.feedback_general: HCl, HNO₃, and HClO₄ (along with HBr, HI, and H₂SO₄ for its first proton) ionize completely — they are strong acids. Acetic acid, HF, and carbonic acid are weak; the hydroxides listed are strong bases, not acids.

questions.text: The stronger an acid is, the weaker its conjugate base.
questions.feedback_general: True. A strong acid (like HCl) donates its proton readily, so its conjugate base (Cl⁻) has little tendency to take a proton back — it is a very weak base. A larger Ka (smaller pKa) marks a stronger acid.

questions.text: Match each salt to the pH of its aqueous solution (from the strength of its parent acid and base).

answers.left: Sodium acetate, NaC₂H₃O₂ (strong base + weak acid)
Ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl (strong acid + weak base)

questions.feedback_general: Only the ion that is the conjugate of a weak acid or base hydrolyzes. NaCl's ions are both spectators → neutral. Acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid → basic. NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of a weak base and donates a proton → acidic.

questions.text: A buffer resists changes in pH because it contains:

answers.text: A strong acid and a strong base in equal amounts
A weak acid together with its conjugate base (or a weak base with its conjugate acid)

questions.feedback_general: A buffer pairs a weak acid with its conjugate base (e.g., H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻, the blood buffer that holds blood near pH 7.4). The two partners neutralize added acid or base, so the pH barely moves. By the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); when [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKa.

questions.text: An exothermic reaction (ΔH = −60 kJ) has a negative entropy change (ΔS = −0.15 kJ/K). Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, how does raising the temperature affect its spontaneity?

answers.text: It becomes more spontaneous as T rises
It becomes nonspontaneous once T is high enough, because the −TΔS term grows positive
It is nonspontaneous at every temperature

questions.feedback_general: With ΔH negative and ΔS negative, the two terms conflict. At low T the reaction is spontaneous (ΔG < 0), but −TΔS is positive and grows with T; above the crossover temperature (T = ΔH/ΔS = 400 K here) ΔG turns positive and the reaction is no longer spontaneous. A −/− reaction is spontaneous only at low temperature.

questions.text: A reaction mixture is sampled and its reaction quotient Q is found to be larger than K. What will happen, and what is the evidence?

answers.text: The reaction shifts right; there is too little product
The reaction runs in reverse (shifts left toward reactants), because Q > K means the products are over-represented relative to equilibrium
Nothing — the system is already at equilibrium
K increases until it equals Q

questions.feedback_general: Comparing Q to K predicts direction from concentration evidence. Q > K means the product side is too large compared with equilibrium, so the net reaction proceeds in reverse (left) until Q falls back to K. (Q < K would shift right; Q = K is equilibrium.)

questions.text: For the contact-process equilibrium 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −198 kJ (exothermic). Predict the effect of raising the temperature.

answers.text: Shift left, toward SO₂ and O₂, because for an exothermic reaction added heat acts like an added product
No shift; temperature does not affect equilibrium
K stays exactly the same and nothing changes

questions.feedback_general: For an exothermic reaction, heat behaves like a product; adding heat (raising T) pushes the equilibrium left, lowering the SO₃ yield and decreasing K. Like the Haber process, industry must balance this against reaction rate — a real-world compromise.

questions.text: On a concentration-vs-time graph for a reversible reaction, the reactant and product curves change at first and then both become flat (horizontal), while neither has reached zero. The flat region is best interpreted as:

answers.text: The reaction has run out of reactant
The reaction has stopped and both rates are now zero
Dynamic equilibrium — the forward and reverse rates have become equal, so concentrations hold constant
A measurement error in the data

questions.feedback_general: Flat but nonzero concentrations mean the amounts are no longer changing even though both reactions continue — the definition of dynamic equilibrium (equal forward and reverse rates). The curves leveling off without hitting zero is the visual evidence of equilibrium.

questions.text: Two students debate water's role. Student 1: "Water is always a base, because it accepts protons." Student 2: "Water can act as either an acid or a base, depending on its partner." Using the Brønsted-Lowry model, which claim does the evidence support?

answers.text: Student 1 — water only ever accepts protons
Student 2 — water is amphoteric: it donates a proton to NH₃ (acting as an acid) and accepts one from HCl (acting as a base)
Neither — water is never an acid or a base
Both are equally valid because the model is arbitrary

questions.feedback_general: The Brønsted-Lowry model judges acid/base behavior by what a species does in a given reaction. Water accepts H⁺ from HCl (base) and donates H⁺ to NH₃ (acid), so the evidence supports Student 2's amphoteric claim. Weighing which model-based claim the evidence fits is how science settles competing explanations.

questions.text: Two acid solutions are both 0.10 M, but solution X has pH 1.0 and solution Y has pH 3.0. What does this evidence show?

answers.text: X and Y are equally strong acids
X is the stronger acid — at the same concentration it produces far more H₃O⁺ (a lower pH)
Y must be more concentrated than X

questions.feedback_general: At equal concentration, the lower pH (higher [H₃O⁺]) reveals a greater degree of ionization, so X is the stronger acid. pH lets you compare acid strength from measured evidence, keeping strength (degree of ionization) distinct from concentration.

questions.text: Adding a small amount of strong acid to a buffer changes its pH only slightly. The best explanation is that:

answers.text: The strong acid does not react at all in a buffer
The buffer's conjugate base neutralizes the added H⁺, so [H₃O⁺] — and therefore pH — barely changes
The buffer raises the value of Kw
The buffer turns the strong acid into pure water with no other effect

questions.feedback_general: A buffer holds a weak acid and its conjugate base. The conjugate base consumes added H⁺ (and the weak acid consumes added OH⁻), so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] — and thus pH by pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) — shifts only a little.

questions.text: In the titration of a strong acid with a strong base, the pH curve rises slowly at first, then leaps almost vertically over a small added volume before leveling off high. The near-vertical jump marks:

answers.text: The equivalence point, where essentially all the acid has been neutralized (pH ≈ 7 for a strong–strong titration)
The point where the base has been completely used up
A dilution error in the procedure

questions.feedback_general: The steep vertical region is the equivalence point: the moles of added base equal the moles of acid originally present. For a strong acid–strong base titration the equivalence pH is about 7, and an indicator such as phenolphthalein changes color within that jump to mark the endpoint.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 8.01 — Review of Redox & Balancing Redox Reactions

questions.text: According to OIL RIG, oxidation is best defined as…

answers.text: the gain of electrons, with the oxidation number decreasing
the loss of electrons, with the oxidation number increasing
the gain of oxygen atoms only
the loss of heat to the surroundings

questions.feedback_general: OIL RIG = Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. When a substance is oxidized it loses electrons, and its oxidation number increases.

questions.text: In a redox reaction, the substance that is reduced is the oxidizing agent.
questions.feedback_general: True. The species that is reduced gains electrons, which means it takes them from its partner — causing the partner to be oxidized. An agent is named for what it does to the other substance, so the reduced species is the oxidizing agent.

questions.text: What is the oxidation number of manganese in the permanganate ion, MnO₄⁻? (Oxygen is −2; the ion's overall charge is −1.)
questions.feedback_general: Four oxygens contribute 4 × (−2) = −8. For the whole ion to equal −1, manganese must be +7, because +7 + (−8) = −1. (When MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺, manganese drops from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons.)

questions.text: In the balanced acidic half-reaction MnO₄⁻ + 8 H⁺ + 5 e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H₂O, which step of the half-reaction method explains the 4 H₂O on the product side?

answers.text: Splitting the reaction into two halves

questions.feedback_general: After balancing atoms other than O and H, you balance oxygen by adding H₂O. MnO₄⁻ has four O atoms, so four H₂O appear on the product side. (Then the 8 H from those waters are balanced by 8 H⁺, and finally charge is balanced with electrons.)

questions.text: For the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), match each species to its role.

answers.left: Number of electrons transferred per Zn

questions.feedback_general: Zinc rises 0 → +2 (oxidized, the reducing agent) and hands 2 electrons to copper(II), which falls +2 → 0 (reduced, the oxidizing agent). Oxidation and reduction always occur together — the electrons zinc loses are exactly the electrons copper(II) gains.

questions.text: Chlorate, ClO₃⁻, turns up in some disinfectants — a species not covered in the lesson. Using the oxidation-number rules (O is −2; the ion's overall charge is −1), what is the oxidation number of chlorine in ClO₃⁻?
questions.feedback_general: Three oxygens give 3 × (−2) = −6. For the whole ion to total −1, chlorine must be +5, because +5 + (−6) = −1. The rule is exactly the one you used for MnO₄⁻ — it works on any species, even one you've never seen.

questions.text: A galvanic (voltaic) cell produces electricity by…

answers.text: using an outside power source to force a nonspontaneous reaction
harnessing a spontaneous redox reaction and routing its electrons through a wire
heating two metals until they melt together
storing static charge on two metal plates

questions.feedback_general: A galvanic cell takes a spontaneous redox reaction, separates it into two half-cells, and forces the electrons to travel through an external wire — that flow of electrons is the current. (A cell that uses an outside power source to drive a nonspontaneous reaction is an electrolytic cell.)

questions.text: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode, and the anode is the negative (−) terminal.
questions.feedback_general: True. "An Ox" — oxidation happens at the anode. Because the anode produces electrons and pushes them out into the wire, it is the negative terminal in a galvanic cell.

questions.text: Through the external wire, the electrons flow…

answers.text: they do not move through the wire at all

questions.feedback_general: Electrons are produced at the anode (oxidation) and consumed at the cathode (reduction), so through the wire they always travel anode → cathode. (The opposite "conventional current" is just an old convention about positive charge.)

questions.text: What is the job of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell?

answers.text: It carries electrons from one electrode to the other
It supplies the metal that gets oxidized
It lets ions move between the half-cells to keep each side electrically neutral
It speeds up the reaction by adding heat

questions.feedback_general: The wire carries electrons; the salt bridge carries ions. As charge builds up in each half-cell, the salt bridge lets ions flow to cancel it, keeping both sides neutral so the current can continue. Remove it and the current stops almost immediately.

questions.text: For the Daniell cell Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s), match each symbol or species to what it means.

answers.right: Boundary between an electrode and its solution

questions.feedback_general: Cell notation runs anode → cathode, left to right. Zinc (left) is the anode where oxidation occurs; copper (right) is the cathode where reduction occurs; the double bar || is the salt bridge; each single bar | marks the boundary between a solid electrode and its solution.

questions.text: A galvanic cell is built from a magnesium electrode in Mg²⁺ solution joined to a silver electrode in Ag⁺ solution. In this cell, magnesium is oxidized (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2 e⁻) and silver ions are reduced (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag). Which statement correctly describes the cell?

answers.text: Magnesium is the cathode, and electrons flow from silver to magnesium
Magnesium is the anode, and electrons flow from magnesium to silver
Silver is the anode, and electrons flow from magnesium to silver
Both electrodes are anodes, so no electrons flow

questions.feedback_general: Oxidation defines the anode ("An Ox"), so the magnesium electrode (where oxidation happens) is the anode; reduction happens at the silver electrode, the cathode. Electrons are produced at the anode and consumed at the cathode, so they travel magnesium (anode) → silver (cathode) — the same anode → cathode rule you learned on the Daniell cell, applied to a cell you've never seen.

questions.text: Why are all electrode potentials measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)?

answers.text: Hydrogen gas is the cheapest reactant to use
A voltmeter can only read a difference between two electrodes, so a common reference is needed
The SHE is the only half-reaction that is truly spontaneous
Hydrogen has the most positive reduction potential of any element

questions.feedback_general: You can't measure one electrode's potential alone — a voltmeter needs two terminals and reads only a difference. Defining the SHE as exactly 0.00 V gives every other half-reaction a shared reference, the way sea level fixes the zero for altitude.

questions.text: A half-reaction with a more positive standard reduction potential (E°) is…

answers.text: more easily oxidized and a stronger reducing agent
more easily reduced and a stronger oxidizing agent
unable to take part in a galvanic cell
always the anode in any cell

questions.feedback_general: A more positive E° means the species pulls electrons strongly — it is more easily reduced, which makes it a stronger oxidizing agent. A more negative E° means the opposite (easily oxidized, a good reducing agent).

questions.text: A cell is built from Cu²⁺/Cu (E° = +0.34 V) and Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V). Using E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, the cell potential is…
questions.feedback_general: Copper has the higher E°, so it is the cathode; zinc is the anode. E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = 0.34 + 0.76 = +1.10 V. Watch the double negative — subtracting −0.76 adds 0.76.

questions.text: When a half-reaction is multiplied by a coefficient to balance electrons (for example, doubling it), its standard reduction potential E° is also doubled.
questions.feedback_general: False. E° is an intensive property — a "push per electron" — so it does not change when you scale a half-reaction. Doubling 2 Ag⁺ + 2 e⁻ → 2 Ag still leaves E° = +0.80 V.

questions.text: Match each cell to whether it is spontaneous (galvanic) based on the sign of its E°cell.
questions.feedback_general: A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous as written — a galvanic cell. A negative E°cell means it will not run on its own as written (the reverse reaction is the spontaneous one).

quizzes.title: Reading Check 8.04 — Cell Potential, Free Energy & Equilibrium

questions.text: In the equation ΔG° = −nFE°cell, what does F represent?

answers.text: The temperature of the cell in kelvin
The number of moles of electrons transferred
The Faraday constant, the charge on one mole of electrons (96,485 C/mol)
The equilibrium constant of the reaction

questions.feedback_general: F is the Faraday constant, 96,485 C/mol — the charge carried by one mole of electrons. It converts the cell's "volts per electron" into the reaction's free energy in joules. (n is the moles of electrons; it is the separate factor.)

questions.text: A cell with a positive E°cell has a negative ΔG° and is spontaneous.
questions.feedback_general: True. The minus sign in ΔG° = −nFE° flips the sign: a positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°, which is the spontaneous (galvanic) case.

questions.text: The Zn–Cu cell transfers 2 electrons and has E°cell = +1.10 V. Using ΔG° = −nFE° (F = 96,485 C/mol), ΔG° is approximately…
questions.feedback_general: ΔG° = −(2)(96,485)(1.10) = −212,267 J ≈ −212 kJ. Keep the minus sign and convert joules to kilojoules by dividing by 1000 — the answer is a couple hundred kJ, not a couple hundred thousand.

questions.text: Which set of signs all describe the same spontaneous, product-favored reaction?
questions.feedback_general: The three quantities lock together: E°cell > 0 ⟺ ΔG° < 0 ⟺ K > 1 — spontaneous and products favored. Reverse all three signs for a reaction that won't go on its own.

questions.text: Match each cell potential to what it tells you about ΔG° and the reaction.

answers.left: A reaction with a large negative ΔG° but a very slow rate
answers.right: Direction is favorable, but speed is a separate question (kinetics)

questions.feedback_general: Voltage and free energy tell you the direction of change, not the speed. A reaction can be strongly spontaneous (big negative ΔG°, positive E°) yet extremely slow — speed is governed by kinetics, the next topic in this module.

quizzes.title: Module 8 Checkpoint 1 — Redox, Galvanic Cells & Cell Potential (Lessons 8.01–8.04)

questions.text: In a redox reaction, oxidation is best defined as:

answers.text: The gain of electrons (oxidation number decreases)
The loss of electrons (oxidation number increases)

questions.feedback_general: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). When a species loses electrons its oxidation number rises. The species that is oxidized is the reducing agent.

questions.text: What is the oxidation number of manganese in the permanganate ion, MnO₄⁻? (Oxygen is usually −2; the charges must sum to the ion's overall charge.)
questions.feedback_general: Four oxygens at −2 give −8. For the ion to total −1, Mn must be +7: (+7) + (−8) = −1. This is why permanganate is such a strong oxidizing agent — Mn is at its highest oxidation state.

questions.text: In the balanced reaction MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, the oxidizing agent is:

answers.text: MnO₄⁻ (it is reduced, so it oxidizes something else)

questions.feedback_general: Mn goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺ — it is reduced, so MnO₄⁻ is the oxidizing agent. Meanwhile each Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ loses an electron (oxidized), making Fe²⁺ the reducing agent. The species that is reduced is always the oxidizing agent.

questions.text: In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, a spontaneous redox reaction is used to produce electrical energy.
questions.feedback_general: True. A galvanic cell harnesses a spontaneous redox reaction (E°cell > 0) and routes the electrons through an external wire, turning chemical energy into electrical energy. (An electrolytic cell does the reverse — it uses electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.)

questions.text: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Through the external wire, electrons flow:

answers.text: They do not move; only ions move

questions.feedback_general: Electrons are released by oxidation at the anode and travel through the wire to the cathode, where reduction consumes them (an aid: "an ox, red cat" — anode oxidation, reduction cathode). In a galvanic cell the anode is the negative terminal and the cathode is positive. The salt bridge keeps each half-cell electrically neutral.

questions.text: The cell notation Zn(s) | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu(s) describes the Daniell cell. In this notation, the species written on the left of the double line (||) is:
questions.feedback_general: By convention the anode (oxidation) is written on the left, the cathode (reduction) on the right, and the double bar || is the salt bridge. Here Zn is oxidized (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and Cu²⁺ is reduced (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu): overall Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

questions.text: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is important because it:

answers.text: Has the most positive reduction potential of any electrode
Is assigned a standard reduction potential of exactly 0.00 V as the reference
Cannot be used in real measurements

questions.feedback_general: Because absolute electrode potentials can't be measured directly, chemists define the SHE as 0.00 V and measure every other electrode against it. A more positive E° means a stronger tendency to be reduced (a stronger oxidizing agent).

questions.text: Using E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, the standard cell potential of the Daniell cell (Cu is the cathode, Zn is the anode) is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode =
questions.feedback_general: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. A positive E°cell confirms the reaction is spontaneous, so the cell is galvanic. Note that E° is intensive — it does not change if you double the coefficients.

questions.text: The relationship between cell potential and free energy is ΔG° = −nFE°cell (F = 96,485 C/mol). This means that a cell with a positive E°cell has:

answers.text: A positive ΔG° and is non-spontaneous
A negative ΔG° and is spontaneous

questions.feedback_general: The minus sign flips the sign: a positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°, which means the reaction is spontaneous and products are favored (K > 1). This is the central link: E°cell > 0 ⟺ ΔG° < 0 ⟺ K > 1.

questions.text: Match each value of E°cell to what it tells you about the cell.

answers.right: The equation linking cell potential to free energy

questions.feedback_general: The signs march together through ΔG° = −nFE°cell. A positive cell voltage powers a galvanic cell (negative ΔG°, products favored); a negative voltage describes a reaction that must be driven (electrolysis); a zero voltage is equilibrium.

questions.text: A student combines two half-cells and calculates E°cell = −0.42 V. What is the correct conclusion?

answers.text: The reaction is spontaneous as written; ΔG° < 0
The reaction is non-spontaneous as written (ΔG° > 0); it would run in the reverse direction, or must be driven by outside power
The reaction is at equilibrium, since any E°cell means no net change
E°cell can never be negative, so the student made an error

questions.feedback_general: A negative E°cell means ΔG° = −nFE°cell is positive — non-spontaneous in the written direction (K < 1). The reaction as written won't run on its own; the reverse reaction is the spontaneous one, or an external power source must drive it (electrolysis). E°cell can absolutely be negative — that is exactly what defines an electrolytic, rather than galvanic, direction.

questions.text: A battery is best described as…

answers.text: a device that stores electricity as a static charge
one or more galvanic cells packaged to deliver portable electrical energy
a cell that always requires an external power source to operate
a container of acid with no electrodes

questions.feedback_general: A battery is simply one or more galvanic cells in a convenient case, sometimes stacked in series so their voltages add.

questions.text: Which of these is a primary (single-use) cell that cannot be recharged?

answers.text: the alkaline battery (zinc anode, MnO₂ cathode)

questions.feedback_general: The alkaline battery is a primary cell — its reaction can't be cleanly reversed, so it is discarded when flat. Lead-acid and lithium-ion are rechargeable (secondary) cells.

questions.text: A secondary cell can be recharged because its redox reaction can be reversed by pushing current through it from an outside source.
questions.feedback_general: That is exactly what makes a cell rechargeable. The lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries are secondary cells; an outside current rebuilds their reactants.

questions.text: The overall reaction of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. What makes a fuel cell different from an ordinary battery?

answers.text: It stores all its reactants sealed inside and runs down quickly
It is supplied with a continuous flow of reactants, so it does not run down as long as fuel is fed
It produces no electricity at all
It cannot be used outside a laboratory

questions.feedback_general: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell fed a continuous flow of reactants, so it keeps producing electricity (with water as its only product) as long as fuel arrives.

questions.text: Match each cell to its family.
questions.feedback_general: Alkaline = primary (discarded when flat); lithium-ion = secondary (rechargeable); the H₂–O₂ cell is a fuel cell, fed continuously rather than sealed.

questions.text: A design team needs a power source for a smartphone: it must be lightweight, store a lot of energy, and recharge every night for years. Which cell is the best-justified choice, and why?

answers.text: An alkaline primary cell, because it is cheap and disposable
A lithium-ion secondary cell, because its high energy density and reversible reaction let it stay light while recharging nightly for years
A lead-acid secondary cell, because it is rechargeable — even though it is heavy
A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, because its only product is water

questions.feedback_general: This is an evidence-based match of cell to job. The phone needs a cell that is both rechargeable (secondary) and high in energy density so it stays light — that is lithium-ion. Lead-acid recharges too but is far too heavy; an alkaline cell can't be recharged at all; a fuel cell needs a continuous fuel supply, not a nightly wall charge. "Best" depends on the job's actual demands.

answers.text: the melting of a metal at high temperature
the unwanted oxidation of a metal by its environment — an electrochemical process
the dissolving of a metal in pure water with no oxygen
the reduction of a metal ion back to the pure metal

questions.feedback_general: Corrosion is the unwanted oxidation of a metal by its surroundings — the same anode/cathode chemistry as a galvanic cell, running in tiny natural cells on the metal's surface.

questions.text: The rusting of iron requires both oxygen and water to be present.
questions.feedback_general: Iron in dry air, or in water with no dissolved oxygen, barely rusts. It is the combination of oxygen and water (sped by salt) that produces rust, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

questions.text: Why does a gold ring resist corrosion while an iron nail rusts?

answers.text: Gold is much harder than iron
Gold is very difficult to oxidize, so air and water cannot take its electrons
Gold reacts instantly with oxygen to form a protective rust
Gold contains no electrons to lose

questions.feedback_general: Gold (like platinum) is extremely hard to oxidize, so ordinary air and water can't remove its electrons — it stays bright. Iron is easily oxidized, so it corrodes.

questions.text: A sacrificial anode (a block of magnesium or zinc bolted to a steel structure) protects the steel because…

answers.text: it forms a waterproof paint layer over the steel
it is a more active metal that is oxidized preferentially, corroding instead of the steel
it makes the steel impossible to oxidize forever
it heats the steel so corrosion cannot occur

questions.feedback_general: The more active metal becomes the anode of the corrosion cells and is consumed, forcing the protected steel to be the cathode. Replace the block when it's gone — this is cathodic protection.

questions.text: Match each corrosion-prevention method to how it works.

answers.right: Coats iron with zinc, which corrodes first
Seals the surface from air and water
Alloyed chromium forms a protective oxide

distractors: Heats the metal to stop oxidation
questions.feedback_general: Galvanizing = zinc coating that corrodes before the iron; paint/oil/plastic = a barrier from air and water; stainless steel = alloying, where chromium forms a protective oxide layer.

questions.text: A block of zinc and a block of iron are bolted firmly together and left outdoors in damp, salty air. Predict which metal corrodes first, and what happens to the other.

answers.text: The iron corrodes first, because it is the larger structure
The zinc corrodes first, because it is more easily oxidized (more active) — and this protects the iron
Both corrode at exactly the same rate, because they are touching
Neither corrodes, because two metals in contact cancel each other out

questions.feedback_general: Zinc is more active (more easily oxidized) than iron, so it becomes the anode of the corrosion cell and corrodes first — the very reasoning behind a sacrificial anode. The iron is forced to be the cathode and is protected for as long as the zinc lasts.

answers.text: produce electricity from a spontaneous reaction
speed up a reaction without changing its direction

questions.feedback_general: Electrolysis spends electricity to push a non-spontaneous reaction uphill — the reverse of a galvanic cell. The device is an electrolytic cell.

questions.text: In both galvanic and electrolytic cells, oxidation always happens at the anode and reduction always happens at the cathode.
questions.feedback_general: Anode = oxidation and cathode = reduction in either cell. What flips between the two cell types is the sign of the terminals (electrolytic: anode +, cathode −).

questions.text: The charge passed during an electrolysis is found from Q = I · t. For a current of 2.0 A flowing for 1.0 hour, the charge is…
questions.feedback_general: Convert time to seconds first: 1.0 h = 3600 s. Then Q = I · t = 2.0 A × 3600 s = 7200 C. Always put the time in seconds before computing Q.

questions.text: To convert the charge passed into moles of electrons, you divide by the Faraday constant, which is…
questions.feedback_general: F = 96,485 coulombs per mole of electrons. moles of e⁻ = Q ÷ F, then use the half-reaction's electron ratio to get moles (and mass) of metal.

questions.text: Match each cell feature to the correct cell type.

answers.left: Produces electricity from a spontaneous reaction
The anode is the positive terminal

questions.feedback_general: An electrolytic cell needs outside power and has a positive anode; a galvanic cell makes electricity from a spontaneous reaction (E°cell > 0) and has a negative anode.

questions.text: A current of 1.00 A flows for 1.00 hour through a copper(II) solution (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; Cu = 63.55 g/mol). Approximately what mass of copper is deposited?
questions.feedback_general: Run the chain: time in seconds, 1.00 h = 3600 s; Q = I·t = 1.00 A × 3600 s = 3600 C; mol e⁻ = 3600 ÷ 96,485 = 0.0373; Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻ per atom, so mol Cu = 0.0373 ÷ 2 = 0.01866; mass = 0.01866 × 63.55 ≈ 1.19 g. Trap-check: 2.37 g means you forgot to divide by 2; 0.020 g means you left the time in minutes.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 8.08 — Reaction Rates & Factors Affecting Rate

questions.text: A reaction rate measures:

answers.text: the amount of energy a reaction releases
the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time
the total mass of product formed

questions.feedback_general: Rate is how fast concentrations change — the change in concentration per unit time, usually in M/s (mol·L⁻¹·s⁻¹). Energy released and spontaneity are separate (thermodynamic) ideas.

questions.text: Steel wool burns in seconds, but a solid iron beam rusts over years, even though both are iron reacting with oxygen. Which factor best explains the difference?

answers.text: the iron beam is not spontaneous
the surface area exposed to oxygen

questions.feedback_general: Steel wool is a tangle of thin threads, exposing an enormous surface to oxygen, so it reacts fast. The beam hides most of its iron inside, so only its thin skin reacts — same chemistry, far slower rate, set by surface area.

questions.text: Which change would generally slow down a reaction?

answers.text: increasing the concentration of a reactant
grinding a solid reactant into powder

questions.feedback_general: Lowering the temperature slows the particles, so they collide less often and with less energy — the reaction slows. The other three changes all speed reactions up.

questions.text: Because a reaction is spontaneous, it must also be fast.
questions.feedback_general: Spontaneity (thermodynamics) tells you only the direction nature favors, not the speed. A spontaneous reaction can be extremely slow — diamond turning to graphite, or iron rusting. Speed is the separate question of kinetics.

questions.text: Match each change to its effect on the reaction's rate.

answers.left: Increase the concentration of a reactant
Grind a solid reactant into fine powder

questions.feedback_general: Higher concentration → more frequent collisions (faster). More surface area → more contact (faster). Lower temperature → slower, less energetic collisions (slower).

questions.text: A chemist needs a slow reaction between a solid metal and an acid to finish faster, but must keep the temperature exactly the same. Which single change would speed the reaction up the most without changing the temperature?

answers.text: Cool the acid in an ice bath
Use the metal as one large solid lump
Grind the metal into a fine powder

questions.feedback_general: Grinding the metal into powder increases its surface area, exposing far more atoms to the acid at once — more collisions per second, so a faster reaction — and it changes nothing about the temperature. Cooling and diluting would both slow the reaction, and a single large lump has the least surface area.

quizzes.title: Reading Check 8.09 — Rate Laws & Collision Theory

questions.text: In a rate law of the form rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, the exponents m and n (the reaction orders) are found by:

answers.text: copying the coefficients from the balanced equation
experiment — measuring how the rate responds to concentration changes
reading them off the periodic table

questions.feedback_general: The orders must come from experimental data, never from the balanced equation's coefficients. This is the single most important — and most often missed — idea about rate laws.

questions.text: In an experiment, doubling [A] (with everything else held constant) causes the rate to quadruple (×4). The reaction is therefore:
questions.feedback_general: Doubling raises the rate by 2 to the power of the order. Since 2² = 4, a quadrupling means second order in A.

questions.text: According to collision theory, a collision will lead to a reaction only if the particles:

answers.text: have enough energy (at least the activation energy) **and** the correct orientation
have enough energy, regardless of orientation
have the correct orientation, regardless of energy

questions.feedback_general: Both conditions are required. A collision must carry at least the activation energy (Eₐ) and be aimed so the right atoms meet. Most collisions fail one test or the other.

questions.text: The rate constant k stays exactly the same regardless of temperature.
questions.feedback_general: k increases as temperature rises (the Arrhenius relationship, k = A·e^(−Eₐ/RT)). It is constant only at a given temperature, which is why heating a reaction speeds it up so strongly.

questions.text: Match what the data show (when one reactant's concentration is doubled) to the reaction order in that reactant.
questions.feedback_general: Doubling gives 2 raised to the order: 2¹ = 2 (first), 2² = 4 (second), 2⁰ = 1 (zero). The factor the rate changes by tells you the order directly.

questions.text: A reaction depends on a single reactant, X. Two trials are run at the same temperature: What is the order in X?
questions.feedback_general: From Trial 1 to Trial 2, [X] doubles (0.10 → 0.20) while the rate goes ×4 (0.020 → 0.080). Since 2² = 4, the reaction is second order in X. Note you had to read this from the data, not from any equation.

questions.text: A reaction mechanism is:

answers.text: the balanced equation for the overall reaction
the step-by-step sequence of elementary steps by which a reaction actually occurs
the amount of energy a reaction releases
a list of all possible products

questions.feedback_general: The mechanism is the "how" — the sequence of elementary steps that add up to the overall equation. The balanced equation is only the "what" (start and finish).

questions.text: In a multi-step mechanism, the overall reaction rate is controlled by:

answers.text: the slowest elementary step (the rate-determining step)
the average of all the steps

questions.feedback_general: The slowest step is the bottleneck — like the slowest worker on an assembly line, it sets the pace for the whole reaction. It is called the rate-determining step.

questions.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by:

answers.text: raising the temperature of the reactants
increasing the concentration of the reactants
providing an alternate pathway with a lower activation energy
being used up to release extra energy

questions.feedback_general: A catalyst opens a lower-Eₐ pathway, so more collisions succeed and the rate rises. It is not consumed — it is regenerated by the end.

questions.text: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction but does not change ΔG, the equilibrium position, or the identity of the products.
questions.feedback_general: A catalyst changes only the rate. Because it lowers the barrier for the forward and reverse directions equally, it gets you to the same destination sooner without changing the destination.

questions.text: Match each kinetics term to its description.

answers.right: The slowest elementary step, which sets the overall rate
Made in one step and consumed in a later step; not in the overall equation
Lowers the activation energy and is not consumed

questions.feedback_general: The rate-determining step is the slow bottleneck; an intermediate is made then used up (so it cancels out of the overall equation); a catalyst lowers Eₐ and is regenerated.

questions.text: An energy-profile diagram shows a reaction's uncatalyzed path as a tall hill between reactants and products. A second, lower hill is drawn between the same reactants and the same products. The lower hill represents:

answers.text: a reaction that releases more energy overall
the catalyzed path, with a lower activation energy
a completely different reaction with different products
the same reaction simply run at a lower temperature

questions.feedback_general: A lower hill between the same start and finish is the catalyzed path — the catalyst opens a route with a smaller activation energy, so more collisions succeed and the rate rises. The reactants, products, and the energy released (ΔG) are unchanged; only the barrier — and therefore the speed — is lower.

questions.text: A primary battery (such as a common alkaline cell) differs from a secondary battery in that a primary battery:

answers.text: Is rechargeable, while a secondary battery is not
Is single-use and not practically rechargeable, while a secondary battery can be recharged

questions.feedback_general: A primary cell (e.g., the alkaline cell: Zn anode / MnO₂ cathode, ~1.5 V) runs its redox reaction once and is discarded. A secondary cell (lead-acid, lithium-ion) can be recharged by driving the reaction backward with an outside current.

questions.text: A typical car battery is a lead-acid battery rated at about 12 V. Given that each lead-acid cell produces about 2 V, how many cells are connected in series?
questions.feedback_general: Each lead-acid cell delivers ~2 V, so 6 cells in series give ~12 V (6 × 2 V). Connecting cells in series adds their voltages — the same reason flashlights stack batteries end to end.

questions.text: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell differs from an ordinary battery because it:

answers.text: Stores all of its reactants inside a sealed case
Is continuously supplied with reactants (H₂ and O₂) from outside as it runs

questions.feedback_general: A fuel cell is fed a continuous flow of reactants rather than holding a fixed charge, so it keeps generating electricity as long as fuel is supplied. Its overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — the only product is water.

answers.text: A useful, deliberate reduction of a metal
An unwanted oxidation of a metal by its environment

questions.feedback_general: Corrosion is the unwanted oxidation of a metal. For iron, rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, and its formation requires both oxygen and water — which is why iron rusts in damp air but not in dry air or pure water alone.

questions.text: A steel pipeline is protected by bolting blocks of magnesium to it. This works because magnesium:

answers.text: Is more easily oxidized than iron, so it corrodes first and protects the steel (a sacrificial anode)
Is more noble (less reactive) than iron
Lowers the temperature of the pipeline

questions.feedback_general: This is cathodic protection with a sacrificial anode. Magnesium is more active (more easily oxidized) than iron, so it gives up its electrons first and corrodes in the steel's place. Galvanizing (a zinc coating) works the same way — the zinc oxidizes before the iron beneath it.

questions.text: Match each iron-protection method to how it works.

answers.right: A barrier coating that keeps out O₂ and water
Coating with zinc, a more active metal that oxidizes first
A more-active metal corrodes in place of the iron
Alloying iron with chromium for corrosion resistance

questions.feedback_general: Barrier methods (paint, oil) block the oxygen and water that rust needs; galvanizing and sacrificial anodes use a more reactive metal that oxidizes preferentially; alloying (stainless steel = iron + chromium) builds corrosion resistance into the metal itself.

True. An electrolytic cell is the reverse of a galvanic cell: instead of a spontaneous reaction producing electricity, an outside current forces a non-spontaneous reaction to occur (E°cell < 0, ΔG° > 0). Electroplating, refining aluminum (Hall–Héroult), and splitting water are all electrolysis.

questions.text: In an electrolytic cell, compared with a galvanic cell:

answers.text: Oxidation moves to the cathode and reduction to the anode
Oxidation still occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, but the electrode **signs are reversed** (anode +, cathode −)

questions.feedback_general: The definitions never change — oxidation is always at the anode and reduction always at the cathode. What flips is the sign: because an external source is now pushing the electrons, the anode is positive and the cathode is negative in an electrolytic cell (the opposite of a galvanic cell).

questions.text: A current of 2.00 A is passed for 3600 s (1 hour) through a solution to plate copper by Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Using Q = I·t, mol e⁻ = Q/F (F = 96,485 C/mol), about how much copper is deposited? (Molar mass Cu ≈ 63.5 g/mol.)
questions.feedback_general: Q = I·t = 2.00 × 3600 = 7200 C; mol e⁻ = 7200 ÷ 96,485 = 0.0746 mol. Because Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons, mol Cu = 0.0746 ÷ 2 = 0.0373 mol; mass = 0.0373 × 63.5 ≈ 2.37 g. Forgetting to divide by 2 (the electron-to-product ratio) gives the wrong answer A.

questions.text: In Faraday's-law calculations, the order is: charge Q = I·t, then moles of electrons = Q / F, then use the electron-to-product ratio from the half-reaction to find moles (and mass) of product.
questions.feedback_general: True. That three-step chain — current × time → coulombs → moles of electrons → moles of product — is the heart of every electrolysis quantity problem. The half-reaction's coefficient (e.g., the 2 in Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) sets the electron-to-product ratio.

questions.text: An engineer needs a cell for a backup power bank that will be charged and discharged thousands of times, sits in a fixed cabinet (so weight does not matter), and where low cost is the top priority. Which choice is best justified by the evidence?

answers.text: An alkaline primary cell, because it is cheap
A lead-acid secondary cell — it is rechargeable and inexpensive, and its heavy weight (low energy density) is acceptable because weight does not matter here
A single-use lithium primary cell, because lithium stores a lot of energy
Any cell with E°cell < 0, so it can be recharged

questions.feedback_general: The job needs many recharge cycles (so a secondary cell, ruling out the primary cells in A and C) at low cost with weight irrelevant — exactly where lead-acid shines: cheap, robust, and rechargeable, with its only real drawback (heavy, low energy density) not mattering in a fixed cabinet. D misreads the chemistry: a working cell discharges spontaneously with E°cell > 0; it is recharged by driving it in reverse.

questions.text: In any redox reaction, reduction is:

answers.text: The loss of electrons (oxidation number increases)
The gain of electrons (oxidation number decreases)

questions.feedback_general: OIL RIG — Reduction Is Gain of electrons; the oxidation number goes down. The species reduced is the oxidizing agent; the species oxidized is the reducing agent.

questions.text: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻? (Oxygen is usually −2.)
questions.feedback_general: Four oxygens at −2 give −8. For the ion to total −2, sulfur must be +6: (+6) + (−8) = −2. Remember the rules: a free element is 0, oxygen is usually −2, hydrogen usually +1, and the oxidation numbers sum to the species' charge.

questions.text: For MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, which statement is correct?

answers.text: Fe²⁺ is reduced and is the oxidizing agent
Mn is reduced from +7 to +2, so MnO₄⁻ is the oxidizing agent and Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent

questions.feedback_general: Mn drops from +7 (in MnO₄⁻) to +2 (Mn²⁺): it is reduced, so MnO₄⁻ is the oxidizing agent. Each Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ loses one electron (oxidized), so Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent. Five Fe²⁺ supply the five electrons that one MnO₄⁻ gains.

questions.text: When balancing a half-reaction in acidic solution, you balance oxygen by adding H₂O, balance hydrogen by adding H⁺, and balance the charge by adding electrons (e⁻).
questions.feedback_general: True. The acidic half-reaction method: balance the main atoms first, add H₂O to balance O, add H⁺ to balance H, then add e⁻ to balance charge. Multiplying the two half-reactions so the electrons cancel gives the balanced overall equation.

questions.text: In a galvanic cell, the anode is the electrode where:

answers.text: Reduction occurs and it is the positive terminal
Oxidation occurs and it is the negative terminal

questions.feedback_general: Oxidation always happens at the anode; in a galvanic cell the anode is the negative terminal (it releases electrons). Reduction happens at the cathode, the positive terminal. Electrons travel anode → cathode through the wire.

questions.text: For the Daniell cell written Zn(s) | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu(s), the overall spontaneous reaction is:
questions.feedback_general: Zinc (left of the ||, the anode) is oxidized: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Copper(II) (right, the cathode) is reduced: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Adding them gives Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

questions.text: The salt bridge in a galvanic cell maintains electrical neutrality in the two half-cells by allowing ions to flow between them.
questions.feedback_general: True. As oxidation builds positive charge in the anode half-cell and reduction removes positive charge in the cathode half-cell, the salt bridge lets ions migrate to keep both sides neutral. Without it, charge buildup would halt the cell almost immediately.

questions.text: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is assigned a standard reduction potential of:
questions.feedback_general: The SHE is defined as exactly 0.00 V so that every other electrode can be measured relative to it. A more positive E° means a greater tendency to be reduced — a stronger oxidizing agent.

questions.text: Given E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, which species is the stronger oxidizing agent?

answers.text: Ag⁺ (more positive E° = more easily reduced)

questions.feedback_general: The more positive the standard reduction potential, the more readily the species is reduced, and the stronger an oxidizing agent it is. Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) is reduced more readily than Cu²⁺ (+0.34 V), so Ag⁺ is the stronger oxidizing agent.
