questions.text: Using E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, with Cu the cathode and Zn the anode, E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is:
questions.feedback_general: E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous, so the Daniell cell is galvanic. E° is intensive — doubling the coefficients does not change it.

questions.text: Standard cell potential E° is an intensive property: multiplying all the coefficients in the balanced reaction by 2 does not change the value of E°cell.
questions.feedback_general: True. Cell potential is energy per unit charge, so it does not scale with the amount of substance. Doubling the equation doubles the electrons transferred (n) and the total energy, but E°cell stays the same. (ΔG°, by contrast, does scale.)

questions.text: The equation linking cell potential to free energy is:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG° = −nFE°cell, where n is the moles of electrons transferred and F = 96,485 C/mol. The minus sign means a positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG° — spontaneous.

questions.text: For the Daniell cell, n = 2 and E°cell = +1.10 V. Using ΔG° = −nFE°cell (F = 96,485 C/mol), ΔG° is approximately:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG° = −(2)(96,485)(1.10) = −212,267 J ≈ −212 kJ. The negative value confirms a spontaneous (galvanic) reaction. A positive E°cell always gives a negative ΔG° and K > 1 — the three travel together.

questions.text: Match each cell condition to its consequences (the signs travel together).
questions.feedback_general: Through ΔG° = −nFE°cell and ΔG° = −RT ln K, a positive voltage means a spontaneous reaction with products favored; a negative voltage means the reaction must be driven (electrolysis); zero voltage is equilibrium.

questions.text: Which describes a secondary battery?

answers.text: A single-use cell that cannot be recharged
A rechargeable cell, such as lead-acid or lithium-ion, restored by driving the reaction backward
A cell that produces no voltage
A cell fed continuous reactants from outside

questions.feedback_general: A secondary cell is rechargeable: an external current drives the spontaneous discharge reaction in reverse (electrolysis) to regenerate the reactants. Lead-acid (~2 V/cell) and lithium-ion are secondary; the alkaline cell is primary (single-use).

questions.text: The overall reaction of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is:
questions.feedback_general: In an H₂–O₂ fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidized and oxygen is reduced, combining to form water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Because reactants are fed continuously, the cell produces electricity as long as fuel flows, and its only product is water.

questions.text: The rusting of iron requires:

answers.text: Neither — iron rusts in a vacuum

questions.feedback_general: Rust (hydrated Fe₂O₃·xH₂O) forms only when both oxygen and water are present, which is why iron corrodes in damp air but not in dry air or in oxygen-free water. Corrosion is the unwanted oxidation of the metal.

questions.text: A zinc coating protects the steel beneath it even if the coating is scratched, because zinc:

answers.text: Is less reactive than iron, so it stays intact
Is more easily oxidized than iron, so it corrodes first and spares the iron
Conducts heat away from the steel

questions.feedback_general: Galvanizing relies on the same principle as a sacrificial anode: zinc is more active (more easily oxidized) than iron, so it gives up electrons preferentially and corrodes first, protecting the steel even where the coating is broken. A more-active metal sacrificing itself is cathodic protection.

questions.text: A current of 2.00 A flows for 3600 s through CuSO₄ solution, depositing copper by Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. With Q = I·t and mol e⁻ = Q/F (F = 96,485 C/mol; Cu ≈ 63.5 g/mol), the mass of copper deposited is about:
questions.feedback_general: Q = 2.00 × 3600 = 7200 C; mol e⁻ = 7200 ÷ 96,485 = 0.0746 mol; because Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻, mol Cu = 0.0373 mol; mass = 0.0373 × 63.5 ≈ 2.37 g. Forgetting to divide by 2 (the electron-to-product ratio) double-counts and gives ~4.74 g.

questions.text: Match each electrochemical cell or process to its description.

answers.right: External power drives a non-spontaneous reaction (E°cell < 0)

questions.feedback_general: A galvanic cell produces electricity from a spontaneous reaction; an electrolytic cell consumes electricity to drive a non-spontaneous one. Recharging a secondary battery is electrolysis applied to a galvanic cell — driving the discharge reaction in reverse.

questions.text: Which change will generally increase the rate of a chemical reaction?

answers.text: Decreasing the concentration of a reactant
Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant

questions.feedback_general: Rate rises with higher concentration, higher temperature, greater surface area, addition of a catalyst, and the nature of the reactants. Greater surface area (e.g., a powder vs a lump) exposes more particles to collide, speeding the reaction.

questions.text: For rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, an experiment shows that doubling [A] (with [B] fixed) multiplies the rate by 4. The order with respect to A is:
questions.feedback_general: Doubling [A] and seeing the rate ×4 means rate ∝ [A]² — second order in A (2² = 4). By the method of initial rates: ×1 → zero order, ×2 → first order, ×4 → second order. Reaction orders are found experimentally, not from the balanced coefficients.

questions.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction because it:

answers.text: Is consumed in the reaction, supplying energy
Provides an alternate pathway with a lower activation energy (Eₐ), without being used up and without changing ΔG or the products
Raises the activation energy so fewer collisions are needed
Shifts the equilibrium toward the products

questions.feedback_general: A catalyst offers an alternate route with a lower Eₐ, so more collisions succeed and the reaction goes faster. It is not consumed, it speeds the forward and reverse directions equally, and it does not change ΔG, K, the equilibrium position, or the products — it changes only the rate. (Collision theory: a successful collision needs enough energy and the correct orientation; Arrhenius: k = A·e^(−Eₐ/RT).)

questions.text: Use this ranking of standard reduction potentials: E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.37 V. Which pairing (cathode/anode) produces the largest positive E°cell?
questions.feedback_general: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is largest when you pair the most positive reduction potential (Ag⁺, the best oxidizing agent → cathode) with the most negative one (Mg, the most easily oxidized → anode): (+0.80) − (−2.37) = +3.17 V. Option D gives only +2.71 V. The most positive minus the most negative always maximizes the voltage.

questions.text: A galvanic cell is drawn with a nickel electrode in Ni²⁺ solution wired through a voltmeter and salt bridge to a silver electrode in Ag⁺ solution. Given E°(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.25 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, which statement correctly reads the diagram?

answers.text: Ni is the cathode, and electrons flow from Ag to Ni
Ag is the cathode (reduction) and Ni is the anode (oxidation); electrons flow Ni → Ag; E°cell = +1.05 V
Both electrodes act as anodes, so no current flows
E°cell is negative, so the cell is electrolytic

questions.feedback_general: The more positive reduction potential (Ag⁺, +0.80 V) is reduced, so silver is the cathode; nickel (−0.25 V) is oxidized at the anode. Electrons always leave the anode and travel to the cathode (Ni → Ag). E°cell = (+0.80) − (−0.25) = +1.05 V — positive, so the cell is spontaneous (galvanic), not electrolytic.

questions.text: A design team must choose a cell for a wall thermostat that draws very little current, may sit unused for years, and is thrown away when spent. Which choice is best justified by the evidence?

answers.text: Lithium-ion, because it has the highest energy density
A lead-acid cell, because it is rechargeable
An alkaline primary cell — it is cheap and shelf-stable, and the device's low, one-time energy demand makes high energy density and rechargeability unnecessary
A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, because its only product is water

questions.feedback_general: Matching the cell to the job is the point: a low-drain, disposable device wastes the cost and materials of a high-energy-density or rechargeable cell. A cheap, shelf-stable alkaline primary cell (~1.5 V) fits the demand and the budget — the responsible engineering choice weighs cost and resources against what the device actually needs.

questions.text: For A + B → products (rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ), the method of initial rates gives: What is the overall reaction order?

answers.text: Second order overall (second order in A, zero order in B)

questions.feedback_general: Compare experiments 1→2: [A] doubles, rate ×4, so 2ᵐ = 4 → m = 2. Compare 1→3: [B] doubles, rate is unchanged, so 2ⁿ = 1 → n = 0. Overall order = m + n = 2. Orders come from the data, not from the coefficients.

questions.text: A reaction-coordinate (energy-profile) diagram shows the reactants higher in energy than the products, with an energy barrier between them. A second, lower barrier is drawn for the same reaction with a catalyst. Which reading of the diagram is correct?

answers.text: The catalyst lowers the activation energy (the barrier) but leaves the reactant and product energies — and therefore ΔG — unchanged
The catalyst raises the activation energy, so the reaction slows
The catalyst lowers ΔG, making the reaction more product-favored
The reaction is endothermic, because the products are lower than the reactants

questions.feedback_general: A catalyst provides an alternate pathway with a lower Eₐ (the shorter barrier), speeding the reaction, but it does not move the reactant or product energy levels, so ΔG (and K) are unchanged. Because the products sit below the reactants, energy is released — the reaction is exothermic, making D wrong.

questions.text: What is the oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion, Cr₂O₇²⁻? (Oxygen is usually −2.)
questions.feedback_general: Seven oxygens at −2 give −14. The two chromium atoms must together be +12 for the ion to total −2: (+12) + (−14) = −2. Because there are two Cr atoms, each is +12 ÷ 2 = +6 (not +12 — that is the total for both). Dichromate, like permanganate, is a strong oxidizing agent with Cr near its highest oxidation state.

questions.text: In the nuclide notation ¹⁴₆C, what does the subscript 6 (the atomic number, Z) tell you?

answers.text: The number of protons, which identifies the element as carbon
The mass of the atom in grams

questions.feedback_general: The atomic number Z is the number of protons, and it alone determines which element the atom is. The mass number A (the superscript) is protons + neutrons.

questions.text: Two atoms have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They are best described as:
questions.feedback_general: Isotopes share the same atomic number Z (same element) but differ in mass number A because they hold different numbers of neutrons.

questions.text: The mass of a nucleus is exactly equal to the combined mass of its separate protons and neutrons.
questions.feedback_general: A nucleus weighs slightly less than its separate nucleons. That missing mass (the mass defect) was converted into the nuclear binding energy that holds the nucleus together, via E = mc².

questions.text: Match each term to its correct description.

answers.right: Short-range attraction that overcomes proton repulsion
Where stable nuclides cluster on an N-vs-Z plot

questions.feedback_general: The strong force holds nucleons together over a tiny range; binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56; stable nuclides fall within the band of stability.

questions.text: Which statement about nuclear stability is correct?

answers.text: Every element has at least one stable isotope
No nuclide beyond Z = 83 (bismuth) is stable; all heavier elements are radioactive
Heavy stable nuclei have far fewer neutrons than protons
Light and heavy stable nuclei both keep an N/Z ratio of exactly 1

questions.feedback_general: Nothing past Z = 83 is stable. Heavier stable nuclei actually need more neutrons (N/Z rising toward ~1.5) because extra neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding repulsion.

questions.text: Calcium-40 has 20 protons and 20 neutrons (N/Z = 1.0). A uranium nuclide has 92 protons and 146 neutrons (N/Z ≈ 1.6). Using the band of stability and the Z = 83 ceiling, which prediction is best supported?

answers.text: The calcium nuclide is likely stable, and the uranium nuclide is radioactive
Both are certainly stable, because both contain neutrons

questions.feedback_general: In a rigid container (constant V), raising the temperature speeds the molecules up, so they hit the walls harder and more frequently — pressure rises with absolute temperature (Gay-Lussac). No mass is added; the molecules just move faster.

questions.text: A gas is collected over water at 25 °C; the total pressure is 760 mmHg. The water vapor pressure at 25 °C is 23.8 mmHg. The partial pressure of the dry collected gas is:
questions.feedback_general: The collected gas is mixed with water vapor, so by Dalton's law P_dry gas = P_total − P_water = 760 − 23.8 = 736.2 mmHg. You must subtract the water vapor's contribution.

questions.text: Using Graham's law (rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁)), compare the effusion of helium (4.00 g/mol) and oxygen (32.00 g/mol):

answers.text: They effuse at the same rate

questions.feedback_general: rate_He / rate_O₂ = √(32.00 ÷ 4.00) = √8 = 2.83. The lighter gas effuses faster, so helium escapes through a small opening about 2.83 times faster than oxygen.

questions.text: Real gases deviate most from ideal-gas behavior (PV = nRT) under conditions of:
questions.feedback_general: At high pressure and low temperature, molecules are crowded and slow, so their own volume and their intermolecular attractions — both ignored by the ideal model — matter most. A model is useful precisely where its assumptions hold.

questions.text: Using q = mcΔT (c_water = 4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹), how much heat is needed to warm 50.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C?
questions.feedback_general: q = (50.0 g)(4.184 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹)(80.0 − 20.0 °C) = 50.0 × 4.184 × 60.0 = 12,552 J ≈ 12.6 kJ. Heat scales with mass, specific heat, and the temperature change.

questions.text: For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl, estimate ΔH from bond energies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol) using ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed):
questions.feedback_general: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH ≈ 679 − 862 = −183 kJ. A negative ΔH means the reaction releases energy — it is exothermic.

questions.text: Which substance has only London dispersion forces acting between its molecules?
questions.feedback_general: CH₄ (methane) is nonpolar, so its only intermolecular force is London dispersion. H₂O, NH₃, and HF all hydrogen-bond (H bonded to O, N, or F).

questions.text: Three substances have similar molar masses but boiling points of −89 °C, −19 °C, and +78 °C. The substance boiling at +78 °C most likely:

answers.text: Can form hydrogen bonds (e.g., it contains an –OH group)
Is the lightest of the three

questions.feedback_general: The highest boiling point points to the strongest intermolecular forces. Among molecules of similar mass, hydrogen bonding (as in an alcohol's –OH group) is strongest, so it requires the most energy to boil.

questions.text: A liquid boils when:

answers.text: Its temperature reaches exactly 100 °C in every case
Its vapor pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure
Its density equals that of air

questions.feedback_general: Boiling occurs when a liquid's vapor pressure rises to match the surrounding pressure. Because that external pressure is lower at high altitude, water boils below 100 °C on a mountain.

questions.text: A solid is very hard, does not conduct electricity, and melts at an extremely high temperature (like diamond or quartz). It is best classified as a:
questions.feedback_general: In a covalent network solid, atoms are joined by a continuous web of covalent bonds (diamond, quartz, silicon carbide). Breaking it means breaking covalent bonds, so it is extremely hard and very high-melting.

questions.text: Match each solute to its electrolyte behavior in water.
questions.feedback_general: Soluble ionic salts and strong acids/bases are strong electrolytes; weak acids/bases (like vinegar's acetic acid) partly ionize; molecular compounds like sugar dissolve but form no ions, so they don't conduct.

questions.text: Using ΔT_f = i·K_f·m with K_f(water) = 1.86 °C/m, the freezing point of a 1.00 m NaCl solution (i = 2) is about:
questions.feedback_general: ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 1.00 = 3.72 °C, so the solution freezes at 0 − 3.72 = −3.72 °C. The two ions per formula unit double the depression — which is why salt is spread on icy roads.

questions.text: A beam of light shone through a glass of milk reveals a visible path, but the same beam through salt water does not. This difference identifies milk as a:

answers.text: Colloid (it scatters light — the Tyndall effect)

questions.feedback_general: Colloids have particles large enough to scatter light (the Tyndall effect), so the beam's path is visible (milk, fog, gelatin). True solutions like salt water have particles too small to scatter light, so no beam shows.

questions.text: Which process is expected to increase the entropy of the system?

answers.text: Water vapor condensing on a window
A solid dissolving to form a solution
A gas being cooled and compressed

questions.feedback_general: Dissolving disperses particles and energy, raising entropy. Condensing, compressing/cooling a gas, and freezing all reduce particle freedom and lower entropy. Entropy rises in the order solid < liquid < gas.

questions.text: The Gibbs free energy change is given by:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin) combines enthalpy and entropy into a single spontaneity criterion: ΔG < 0 is spontaneous, ΔG > 0 is nonspontaneous, ΔG = 0 is at equilibrium.

questions.text: For a reaction at 298 K with ΔH = −100 kJ and ΔS = +50 J/K (+0.050 kJ/K), the value of ΔG is:
questions.feedback_general: TΔS = 298 × 0.050 = 14.9 kJ, so ΔG = −100 − 14.9 = −114.9 kJ — spontaneous. Watch the unit conversion: ΔS in J/K must become kJ/K to subtract from ΔH in kJ.

questions.text: Match each sign combination to its temperature dependence for spontaneity.
questions.feedback_general: When ΔH and ΔS push the same direction (−/+ or +/−), temperature can't change the outcome. When they conflict (−/− or +/+), the −TΔS term decides: low T favors enthalpy, high T favors entropy.

questions.text: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol). Which set of conditions would, by Le Châtelier's principle alone, maximize the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
questions.feedback_general: High pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles (4 mol → 2 mol of NH₃). Because the reaction releases heat, low temperature also shifts toward product. In practice industry uses a moderate temperature plus an iron catalyst, since very low temperature makes the reaction far too slow — a real-world compromise between yield and rate.

questions.text: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, which statement about the equilibrium constant K is correct?

answers.text: Pure solids and liquids are included in the K expression
K = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b), and a large K means products are favored
K changes whenever a catalyst is added

questions.feedback_general: K is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient; pure solids and liquids are omitted. A large K (≫ 1) favors products, a small K (≪ 1) favors reactants. A catalyst does not change K.

questions.text: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), at equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.20 M and [HI] = 1.60 M. The value of Kc is:
questions.feedback_general: Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = (1.60)² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 / 0.04 = 64. The HI concentration is squared because of the coefficient 2 in the balanced equation.

questions.text: Under the Brønsted-Lowry definitions, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, the base is:
questions.feedback_general: Water accepts the proton donated by HCl, so water is the Brønsted-Lowry base here and HCl is the acid. Water is amphoteric — it can donate or accept a proton depending on its partner.

questions.text: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M. Its pH, and whether it is acidic or basic, is:
questions.feedback_general: pH = −log[H₃O⁺] = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.00. A pH below 7 (at 25 °C) is acidic. The pOH would be 14.00 − 3.00 = 11.00.

questions.text: In a titration, 25.0 mL of HCl is exactly neutralized by 30.0 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. Using M_aV_a = M_bV_b, the concentration of the HCl is:
questions.feedback_general: mol NaOH = 0.0300 L × 0.100 M = 0.00300 mol = mol HCl (1 : 1); M_HCl = 0.00300 mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.120 M. The strong acid–strong base equivalence point is pH 7.

questions.text: In any redox reaction, reduction is:

answers.text: The loss of electrons (oxidation number increases)
The gain of electrons (oxidation number decreases)

questions.feedback_general: OIL RIG — Reduction Is Gain of electrons; the oxidation number goes down. The species reduced is the oxidizing agent; the species oxidized is the reducing agent. (Redox first appeared as a reaction type back in Module 4.)

questions.text: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻? (Oxygen is usually −2.)
questions.feedback_general: Four oxygens at −2 give −8. For the ion to total −2, sulfur must be +6: (+6) + (−8) = −2. A free element is 0, oxygen is usually −2, and the oxidation numbers sum to the species' charge.

questions.text: In a galvanic cell, the anode is the electrode where:

answers.text: Reduction occurs and it is the positive terminal
Oxidation occurs and it is the negative terminal

questions.feedback_general: Oxidation always happens at the anode; in a galvanic cell the anode is the negative terminal (it releases electrons). Reduction happens at the cathode, the positive terminal. Electrons travel anode → cathode through the wire.

questions.text: Using E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, with Cu the cathode and Zn the anode, E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is:
questions.feedback_general: E°cell = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous, so the Daniell cell is galvanic. E° is intensive — doubling the coefficients does not change it.

questions.text: For the Daniell cell, n = 2 and E°cell = +1.10 V. Using ΔG° = −nFE°cell (F = 96,485 C/mol), ΔG° is approximately:
questions.feedback_general: ΔG° = −(2)(96,485)(1.10) = −212,267 J ≈ −212 kJ. A positive E°cell always gives a negative ΔG° and K > 1 — the three travel together. This is the same free-energy story you met in Module 7, now read off a voltmeter.

questions.text: A zinc coating protects the steel beneath it even if the coating is scratched, because zinc:

answers.text: Is less reactive than iron, so it stays intact
Is more easily oxidized than iron, so it corrodes first and spares the iron
Conducts heat away from the steel

questions.feedback_general: Galvanizing relies on the same principle as a sacrificial anode: zinc is more active (more easily oxidized) than iron, so it gives up electrons preferentially and corrodes first, protecting the steel even where the coating is broken. A more-active metal sacrificing itself is cathodic protection.

questions.text: A current of 2.00 A flows for 3600 s through CuSO₄ solution, depositing copper by Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. With Q = I·t and mol e⁻ = Q/F (F = 96,485 C/mol; Cu ≈ 63.5 g/mol), the mass of copper deposited is about:
questions.feedback_general: Q = 2.00 × 3600 = 7200 C; mol e⁻ = 7200 ÷ 96,485 = 0.0746 mol; because Cu²⁺ needs 2 e⁻, mol Cu = 0.0373 mol; mass = 0.0373 × 63.5 ≈ 2.37 g. Forgetting to divide by 2 double-counts and gives ~4.74 g.

questions.text: For rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, an experiment shows that doubling [A] (with [B] fixed) multiplies the rate by 4. The order with respect to A is:
questions.feedback_general: Doubling [A] and seeing the rate ×4 means rate ∝ [A]² — second order in A (2² = 4). By the method of initial rates: ×1 → zero order, ×2 → first order, ×4 → second order. Reaction orders are found experimentally, not from the balanced coefficients.

questions.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction because it:

answers.text: Is consumed in the reaction, supplying energy
Provides an alternate pathway with a lower activation energy (Eₐ), without being used up and without changing ΔG or the products
Raises the activation energy so fewer collisions are needed
Shifts the equilibrium toward the products

questions.feedback_general: A catalyst offers an alternate route with a lower Eₐ, so more collisions succeed and the reaction goes faster. It is not consumed, it speeds the forward and reverse directions equally, and it does not change ΔG, K, the equilibrium position, or the products — only the rate.

questions.text: For an atom written ²³⁵₉₂U, the number of neutrons is:
questions.feedback_general: Neutrons = A − Z = 235 − 92 = 143. The superscript is the mass number (A); the subscript is the atomic number (Z = protons).

questions.text: Complete and classify: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ?
questions.feedback_general: Balancing A: 238 = 234 + 4. Balancing Z: 92 = 90 + 2. The missing particle is ⁴₂He — an alpha particle. Alpha decay drops the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.text: Which radiation has the greatest penetrating power and requires thick lead or concrete to stop it?
questions.feedback_general: Penetrating power, least to most: alpha (stopped by paper or skin) < beta (a few mm of aluminum) < gamma (highly penetrating; needs thick lead or concrete). Ionizing power runs the other way — alpha is the most ionizing.

questions.text: A wooden artifact has 1/4 of the carbon-14 a living tree of the same size would have. Carbon-14's half-life is about 5730 years. The artifact is approximately:
questions.feedback_general: 1/4 = (1/2)² means two half-lives have passed: 2 × 5730 = 11,460 years. Carbon-14 dating works because a living thing keeps a steady ¹⁴C level; after death the ¹⁴C decays and the fraction left gives the age.

questions.text: Both nuclear fission and fusion release enormous energy because:

answers.text: Electrons are rearranged into lower orbitals
A tiny amount of mass is converted to energy via E = mc²

questions.feedback_general: In both processes the products have slightly less mass than the reactants; that lost mass becomes energy through E = mc². Because c² is enormous, even a tiny mass change releases a huge amount of energy — far more than any chemical (electron-level) reaction.

answers.text: The source is held at arm's length
The source is ingested or inhaled, so it deposits its energy directly inside the body
It is blocked by a sheet of paper
It is emitted by a smoke detector across the room

questions.feedback_general: From outside the body, alpha is stopped by skin or clothing. But if an alpha emitter is taken inside, its high ionizing power and large quality factor make it very damaging to nearby tissue. So the danger depends on radiation type and on whether the source is internal or external — one reason decisions about nuclear medicine and power require an honest weighing of benefits against risks.
